knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weierstrass Minimum-Attainment Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compactness-based attainment for a continuous real-valued function; nonemptiness is necessary for the existence conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let D be a nonempty compact set and let f:D\to\mathbb{R} be continuous. Then there exists x^*\in D such that f(x^*)\leq f(x) for every x\in D.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every continuous real-valued function on a nonempty compact set attains a global minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x^*\in D\ \forall x\in D,\quad f(x^*)\leq f(x).

children.title: Compact-Domain Attainment
children.top_down_role: Attainment on compact feasible domains.

assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a nonempty compact subset of a topological space \(X\).
\(f:K\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is lower semicontinuous and proper on \(K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in K}f(x)\neq\varnothing\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Weierstrass attainment for a proper lower-semicontinuous function on a nonempty compact domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real lower-semicontinuous form of compact-domain Weierstrass attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a nonempty compact subset of a topological space \(X\), and let \(f:K\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous. Then \(m:=\inf_{x\in K}f(x)\) is finite from below and there exists \(\bar x\in K\) such that \(f(\bar x)=m\). Equivalently, \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in K}f(x)\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper lower-semicontinuous objective on a nonempty compact feasible domain attains its minimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Compact-Domain Attainment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem is mathematically precise and fits Compact-Domain Attainment, but no citation with an inspectable locator is supplied. An authoritative source is required before candidate review.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower Bounds on Bounded Sets and Minima on Compact Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consequences of properness and lower semicontinuity in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be proper and lower semicontinuous. For every bounded set \(B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), \(f\) is bounded below on \(B\) by a finite real number. Moreover, for every compact set \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(K\cap\operatorname{dom}f\neq\varnothing\), there exists \(x^*\in K\) such that \(f(x^*)=\min_{x\in K}f(x)\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper lower-semicontinuous extended-real-valued function is finitely bounded below on every bounded subset of R^n and attains a finite minimum on every compact subset meeting its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ bounded},\ \inf_{x\in B}f(x)>-\infty;\qquad \forall K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ compact with }K\cap\operatorname{dom}f\neq\varnothing,\ \operatorname{argmin}_{x\in K}f(x)\neq\varnothing\text{ and }\min_{x\in K}f(x)\in\mathbb{R}.

source_evidence.locator: Max and Min / C. Attainment of a Minimum / Corollary 1.10

children.title: Sequential-Compactness Attainment
children.top_down_role: Attainment through subsequential compactness of minimizing sequences.

assumptions_latex: \(f:K\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and sequentially lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every minimizing sequence has a subsequence converging to some \(\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{K}f\).

notation.meaning: A sequence whose objective values approach the infimum

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct subsequence argument for sequentially compact feasible sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential formulation, without assuming that compactness and sequential compactness coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a nonempty sequentially compact space and let \(f:K\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and sequentially lower semicontinuous. If \((x_n)\subset K\) satisfies \(f(x_n)\to m:=\inf_{x\in K}f(x)\), then some subsequence \((x_{n_k})\) converges to a point \(\bar x\in K\). Sequential lower semicontinuity gives \(f(\bar x)\leq\liminf_k f(x_{n_k})=m\), hence \(f(\bar x)=m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convergent subsequence of any minimizing sequence yields a minimizer when the objective is sequentially lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential-Compactness Attainment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sequential-compactness theorem and content kind fit the leaf, but the statement includes proof steps and has no cited source. Supply an authoritative locator and restate only the theorem claim.

children.title: Topological Compactness Attainment
children.top_down_role: Attainment in nonmetrizable compactness regimes.

assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a nonempty compact topological space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A minimizing net has a convergent subnet whose limit belongs to \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{K}f\).

notation.meaning: A net indexed by a directed set

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: net-based compactness and lower-semicontinuity argument
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Net-based attainment suitable for compact spaces that need not be metrizable or sequentially compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a nonempty compact topological space and let \(f:K\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous. Choose a net \((x_\alpha)\subset K\) with \(f(x_\alpha)\to m:=\inf_{x\in K}f(x)\). Compactness supplies a subnet converging to some \(\bar x\in K\). Lower semicontinuity along convergent nets yields \(f(\bar x)\leq m\), so \(f(\bar x)=m\) and the infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Topological compactness gives a convergent subnet of a minimizing net, and lower semicontinuity makes its limit a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.title: Topological Compactness Attainment

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The net-based theorem correctly targets nonmetrizable compactness, but the statement contains proof narration and no inspectable citation. Supply an authoritative source and retain only the theorem statement.

children.title: Inf-Compactness
children.top_down_role: Compactness localized to objective lower levels.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is inf-compact exactly when \(\{x\in X:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is compact for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).

notation.meaning: Lower level set at height alpha

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard global definition of an inf-compact function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global inf-compactness; relative inf-compactness on a feasible subset is not included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a topological space \(X\), a function \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is called inf-compact if, for every real number \(\alpha\), its lower level set \(L_\alpha(f):=\{x\in X:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is compact in \(X\). Empty lower level sets count as compact. If \(f\) is proper and bounded below, any nonempty lower level set above \(\inf_X f\) localizes every sufficiently accurate minimizing sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An objective is inf-compact when each of its finite lower level sets is compact.
knowledge_statements.title: Inf-Compactness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The core definition fits Inf-Compactness, but no terminology source is cited and the final sentence adds a vaguely quantified minimizing-sequence consequence. A sourced replacement should state the definition separately and quantify any additional property precisely.

children.title: Level-Boundedness Criteria
children.top_down_role: Sublevel-set control of minimizing sequences.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is level-bounded if and only if \(\{x\in\mathbb R^n:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is bounded for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).

notation.meaning: Lower level set at height alpha

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional global level-boundedness and its sequential escape characterization.

source_refs.locator: 9.1.5 Boundedness of level sets p. 826
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proper function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is level-bounded if \(L_\alpha(f):=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is bounded for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\). Equivalently, for every sequence \((x_k)\subset\mathbb R^n\) satisfying \(\|x_k\|\to\infty\), one has \(f(x_k)\to+\infty\). If \(f\) is also lower semicontinuous, every \(L_\alpha(f)\) is compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Level-boundedness means every real lower level set is bounded; equivalently, the objective tends to positive infinity along every sequence escaping to infinity. In finite dimensions, lower semicontinuity then makes the lower level sets compact.
knowledge_statements.title: Level-Boundedness Criteria

source_witnesses.locator: 9.1.5 Boundedness of level sets p. 826
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

children.title: Coercivity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Growth conditions preventing escape to infinity.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Coercivity means \(\|x_k\|\to\infty\Rightarrow f(x_k)\to+\infty\), equivalently every lower level set \(\{x\in X:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\), \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), is norm-bounded.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard norm-coercivity criterion and bounded-sublevel equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm-coercivity, distinct from stronger growth rates such as supercoercivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proper function \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) on a normed space is coercive if, for every sequence \((x_k)\subset X\), \(\|x_k\|\to\infty\) implies \(f(x_k)\to+\infty\). This is equivalent to norm-boundedness of every lower level set \(\{x\in X:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\), where \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\). In finite dimensions, if \(f\) is also lower semicontinuous, these lower level sets are compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A norm-coercive objective diverges to positive infinity along every sequence escaping in norm, equivalently every real lower level set is norm-bounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Coercivity Regimes

children.title: Equivalence Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Settings where the two growth conditions coincide or separate.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is coercive and weakly inf-compact, but it is not inf-compact in the norm topology.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: closed bounded balls are noncompact in infinite-dimensional normed spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows where coercivity ceases to imply norm-topological inf-compactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space and define \(f(x):=\|x\|^2\). Then \(f\) is continuous, proper, and coercive, and its lower level sets are closed and norm-bounded. However, \(L_1(f)=\{x\in H:\|x\|\leq1\}\) is not norm-compact, so \(f\) is not inf-compact for the norm topology. Because \(H\) is reflexive, the same level set is weakly compact; thus compactness depends essentially on the chosen topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In infinite dimensions, coercivity gives bounded sublevels but not norm-compact ones; weak compactness may still survive.
knowledge_statements.title: Equivalence Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Hilbert-space example is a correct failure boundary separating coercivity from norm-topological inf-compactness, and its content kind fits the leaf. No inspectable source locator is supplied.

children.title: Horizon Criteria
children.top_down_role: Asymptotic geometry expressed through horizon objects.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is level-bounded if and only if \(f^\infty(d)>0\) for every \(d\neq0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: finite-dimensional horizon-function characterization of level-boundedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional horizon-function criterion using the epigraphical horizon construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, and let \(f^\infty\) be the function whose epigraph is the horizon cone of \(\operatorname{epi}f\). Then \(f\) is level-bounded if and only if \(f^\infty(d)>0\) for every \(d\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\). Equivalently, the zero sublevel of the horizon function satisfies \(\{d:f^\infty(d)\leq0\}=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper lower-semicontinuous finite-dimensional objective is level-bounded exactly when every nonzero horizon direction has positive horizon value.
knowledge_statements.title: Horizon Criteria

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition has the expected finite-dimensional horizon-function form, but its validity depends on the precise epigraphical horizon definition. No source or exact theorem locator is supplied, so the mathematical version cannot be confirmed reliably.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Horizon criterion for boundedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to every subset of finite-dimensional Euclidean space, including the empty set under the zero-cone convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\),
\[
C\text{ is bounded}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad C^\infty=\{0\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subset of finite-dimensional Euclidean space is bounded if and only if its horizon cone contains only the zero vector.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C\text{ is bounded}\iff C^\infty=\{0\}.

children.title: Recession Criteria
children.top_down_role: Escape directions detected through recession behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is level-bounded if and only if \(f^{0+}(d)>0\) for every \(d\neq0\).

notation.meaning: A point in the effective domain

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: recession-function characterization for proper closed convex functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed convex finite-dimensional specialization of the horizon criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. For any \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\), define \(f^{0+}(d):=\sup_{t>0}[f(x_0+td)-f(x_0)]/t\); this value is independent of \(x_0\). Then \(f\) is level-bounded if and only if \(f^{0+}(d)>0\) for every \(d\neq0\), equivalently \(\{d:f^{0+}(d)\leq0\}=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper closed convex function, level-boundedness is equivalent to strictly positive recession cost in every nonzero direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Recession Criteria

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The closed convex recession criterion fits the leaf, but the base-point-independent formula and strict-positivity equivalence require an authoritative definition and theorem locator. None is supplied.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession Directions and Feasible Rays
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and elementary geometry for an arbitrary, possibly nonconvex Euclidean set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^N\). A vector \(v\in\mathbb R^N\) is a recession direction of \(S\) if there exists \(x\in S\) such that \(x+\tau v\in S\) for every \(\tau\ge0\). The set of all recession directions is denoted \(0^+S\); it is a cone, but need not be convex when \(S\) is nonconvex. A feasible ray of \(S\) is a set \[\{x+\tau v:\tau\ge0\}\] for some \(x\in S\) and \(v\in0^+S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recession direction permits indefinite movement from some point of S while remaining in S. These directions form a cone, which need not be convex for nonconvex S. A feasible ray is the corresponding half-line from a feasible base point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v\in0^+S\iff \exists x\in S\;\forall\tau\ge0,\ x+\tau v\in S;\qquad 0^+S\text{ is a cone and may be nonconvex when }S\text{ is nonconvex.}

children.title: Asymptotic Escape Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where nontrivial escape directions obstruct boundedness.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) attains its minimum although \(f^\infty(0,1)=0\) and its lower level sets are unbounded.

notation.meaning: Quadratic objective constant in the second coordinate

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit convex counterexample separating attainment from level-boundedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A nonpositive asymptotic direction obstructs level-boundedness, but does not by itself obstruct attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\) by \(f(x,y):=x^2\). The function is proper, continuous, and convex, and \(\operatorname*{argmin}f=\{(0,y):y\in\mathbb R\}\), so its minimum is attained. Nevertheless, every nonempty lower level set contains the line \(\{(0,y):y\in\mathbb R\}\), and \(f^\infty(0,1)=0\). Thus failure of the strict horizon or recession criterion proves non-level-boundedness, not necessarily nonattainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-cost escape direction can make sublevels unbounded while a whole affine set of minimizers still exists.
knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Escape Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example correctly shows that attainment does not imply level-boundedness and the failure_boundary kind fits the leaf. It lacks a citation with an inspectable locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex–Concave Hamiltonian Global Sufficiency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A global sufficient optimality condition for a variational problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume that $L$ satisfies the stated convexity condition and that $l$ is convex. Let $p$ be an arc such that $$\begin{bmatrix}-\dot p(t)\\ \dot x(t)\end{bmatrix}\in\partial H(t,x(t),p(t))\quad\text{for a.e. }t,$$ and $$\begin{bmatrix}p(a)\\-p(b)\end{bmatrix}\in\partial l(x(a),x(b)).$$ If, for every $t$, the map $y\mapsto H(t,y,p(t))$ is concave, then $x$ solves $P_B$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the given convexity condition on the Lagrangian, convexity of the endpoint cost, concavity of the Hamiltonian in the state along the costate arc, and the stated Hamiltonian and endpoint subgradient inclusions, the arc is a global solution of the variational problem.
assumptions_latex: L\text{ satisfies the stated convexity condition}.
y\mapsto H(t,y,p(t))\text{ is concave for every }t.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ solves }P_B.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convergence of Ritz approximate infima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Here \(\mu_n\) denotes the approximate infimum associated with the first \(n\) functions of the Ritz trial sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\) be continuous and let the Ritz trial sequence be complete in \(\mathcal M\). If \(\mu_n\) is the corresponding \(n\)-dimensional Ritz approximate infimum and \(\mu=\inf_{y\in\mathcal M}J[y]\), then \(\lim_{n\to\infty}\mu_n=\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the functional is continuous and the Ritz trial sequence is complete, then the infimum values of the finite-dimensional Ritz problems converge to the infimum over the full admissible class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lim_{n\to\infty}\mu_n=\mu

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Completeness of a Ritz trial sequence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Completeness is understood in the norm of the admissible function class \(\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A trial sequence \((\phi_k)_{k\ge 1}\) is complete in \(\mathcal M\) if, for every \(y\in\mathcal M\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist \(n\) and a finite linear combination \(\eta_n\in\operatorname{span}\{\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_n\}\) such that \(\|\eta_n-y\|<\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Ritz trial sequence is complete in the admissible class when every admissible function can be approximated arbitrarily closely in norm by a finite linear combination of trial functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists n\;\exists\eta_n\in\operatorname{span}\{\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_n\}:\ \|\eta_n-y\|<\varepsilon

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Attainment, Strong Duality, and Extremality Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The formulation is conditional on the standing hypotheses and definitions of the referenced primal and dual problems, which are not reproduced in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the primal problem \((5.0)\) and dual problem \((5.9)\), the dual problem has an optimizer \(\bar p^{*}\) and \(\inf(5.0)=\sup(5.9)\). If \(\bar u\) is a primal optimizer, then
\[
\chi_{\mathcal C}(\bar u)+\chi_{\mathcal C}^{*}(\Lambda^{*}\bar p^{*})=\langle\Lambda^{*}\bar p^{*},\bar u\rangle,
\]
and
\[
g(x,\Lambda\bar u(x))+g^{*}(x,-\bar p^{*}(x))=-\bar p^{*}(x)\cdot\Lambda\bar u(x)
\quad\text{for a.e. }x\in\Omega.
\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimizing sequence and direct-method attainment principle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to an extended-real functional on an admissible function class when its infimum is finite and the functional is finite somewhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J:\mathcal M\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) satisfy \(\mu:=\inf_{y\in\mathcal M}J[y]>-\infty\) and \(J[y_0]<+\infty\) for some \(y_0\in\mathcal M\). A sequence \((y_n)\subset\mathcal M\) is minimizing if \(J[y_n]\to\mu\); such a sequence exists. If \(y_n\to\widehat y\in\mathcal M\) and \(J[\widehat y]=\lim_{n\to\infty}J[y_n]\), then \(J[\widehat y]=\mu\), so \(\widehat y\) is a minimizer. Thus the direct method consists of constructing a minimizing sequence, obtaining an admissible limit, and justifying passage of the functional to that limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a functional has a finite infimum and is finite at some admissible function, a sequence of admissible functions whose values approach the infimum exists and is called a minimizing sequence. If that sequence converges to an admissible limit and the functional value passes to the limit, the limit attains the infimum. The direct method therefore requires construction, convergence to an admissible limit, and justified limit passage.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists (y_n)\subset\mathcal M:\ J[y_n]\to\mu,\qquad \bigl(y_n\to\widehat y\in\mathcal M\ \land\ J[\widehat y]=\lim_nJ[y_n]\bigr)\Rightarrow J[\widehat y]=\mu.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a reflexive Banach space, let \(A\subset X\) be closed and convex, and let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}_{\infty}\) be convex and lower semicontinuous. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-perimeter sets and perimeter compactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The compactness conclusion is stated in the fixed bounded-holdall regime implicit in the surrounding set-parametrization context.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subset\mathbb R^N\) be bounded. A measurable set \(E\subseteq D\) is a Caccioppoli set, or set of finite perimeter in \(D\), when \(\chi_E\in BV(D)\), equivalently when \(D\chi_E\) is a finite vector-valued Radon measure. Its perimeter is \(P(E;D)=|D\chi_E|(D)\), which provides the relaxed boundary measure. If \(E_j\subseteq D\) and \(\sup_jP(E_j;D)<\infty\), then a subsequence of \(\chi_{E_j}\) converges in \(L^1(D)\) to the characteristic function of a finite-perimeter set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-perimeter set has a characteristic function of bounded variation, and its perimeter is the total variation of the distributional gradient. In a fixed bounded holdall, a uniform perimeter bound gives subsequential L1 compactness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\,j_k\text{ and a finite-perimeter }E\subseteq D:\ \chi_{E_{j_k}}\to\chi_E\text{ in }L^1(D)

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: uniform tightness is the standard compact-containment criterion for finite measures on Polish spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform tightness for finite nonnegative measures on a Polish space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family \(\mathcal M\) of finite nonnegative Borel measures on a Polish space \(S\) is uniformly tight if and only if, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists a compact set \(K_\varepsilon\subset S\) such that \(\sup_{\mu\in\mathcal M}\mu(S\setminus K_\varepsilon)<\varepsilon\). For probability measures this condition says that one compact set contains at least \(1-\varepsilon\) mass for every member of \(\mathcal M\). For general finite measures, uniform boundedness of \(\mu(S)\) is additionally required in the usual relative-compactness criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform tightness means that, to any tolerance, one compact set captures all but that tolerance of every measure's mass.
knowledge_statements.title: Tightness Criteria

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition correctly states uniform tightness for finite nonnegative measures and fits the leaf, but it has no cited authoritative source or locator.

children.title: Weak Measure Compactness
children.top_down_role: Sequential compactness routes for finite or probability measures.

assumptions_latex: \(S\) is a Polish space and \((\mu_n)\) is a sequence of finite nonnegative Borel measures.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist a finite nonnegative Borel measure \(\mu\) and a subsequence satisfying \(\int_S f\,d\mu_{n_k}\to\int_S f\,d\mu\) for every \(f\in C_b(S)\).

notation.meaning: bounded continuous real-valued functions on the state space

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: this is the sequential finite-measure form of Prokhorov compactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential Prokhorov compactness for uniformly bounded finite measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be Polish and let \((\mu_n)\) be finite nonnegative Borel measures satisfying \(\sup_n\mu_n(S)<\infty\). If \((\mu_n)\) is uniformly tight, then there are a subsequence \((\mu_{n_k})\) and a finite nonnegative Borel measure \(\mu\) such that \(\mu_{n_k}\Rightarrow\mu\); explicitly, \(\int_S f\,d\mu_{n_k}\to\int_S f\,d\mu\) for every \(f\in C_b(S)\). Conversely, every relatively compact family for this narrow topology is uniformly tight and has uniformly bounded total mass.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniformly bounded, uniformly tight finite measures on a Polish space have a narrowly convergent subsequence; relative narrow compactness also forces these conditions.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Measure Compactness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem is the appropriate finite-measure form of Prokhorov compactness, but both directions require an authoritative citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Concentration-Sensitive Compactness
children.top_down_role: Compactness regimes accounting for concentrating mass.

assumptions_latex: \((\mu_n)\) is a sequence of Borel probability measures on \(\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After subselection, exactly one regime occurs: vanishing, tightness modulo translations, or dichotomy into asymptotically separated masses \(\alpha\) and \(1-\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concentration-compactness trichotomy for probability measures on Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For Borel probability measures \((\mu_n)\) on \(\mathbb R^d\), define \(Q_n(R)=\sup_{y\in\mathbb R^d}\mu_n(B_R(y))\). After passing to a subsequence, the concentration functions determine \(\alpha\in[0,1]\) and one of three regimes: if \(\alpha=0\), mass vanishes uniformly on every fixed-radius ball; if \(\alpha=1\), translations \((y_n)\) exist for which the translated measures are tight; if \(0<\alpha<1\), the measures admit, up to arbitrarily small remainder, components of masses approaching \(\alpha\) and \(1-\alpha\) whose supports become mutually separated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A probability-measure sequence either vanishes locally, becomes tight after translation, or splits into two positive masses moving arbitrarily far apart.
knowledge_statements.title: Concentration-Sensitive Compactness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The concentration-compactness role fits the leaf, but the precise trichotomy and dichotomy decomposition cannot be validated without a theorem-level source.

children.title: Mass-Escape Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Loss of compactness through spatial escape or concentration.

assumptions_latex: For \(n\in\mathbb N\), let \(\mu_n=\delta_n\) be the Dirac probability measure at \(n\) on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\mu_n)\) is not tight and has no narrowly convergent subsequence in \(\mathcal P(\mathbb R)\), although \(\int f\,d\mu_n\to0\) for every \(f\in C_c(\mathbb R)\).

notation.meaning: Dirac probability measure at the point n

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: translating Dirac masses are the canonical mass-escape example
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical loss of probability mass at spatial infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mu_n=\delta_n\) on \(\mathbb R\). For every compact \(K\subset\mathbb R\), one has \(\mu_n(K)=0\) for all sufficiently large \(n\); hence \((\mu_n)\) is not tight. It therefore has no narrowly convergent subsequence in the probability space \(\mathcal P(\mathbb R)\). Nevertheless, \(\int_{\mathbb R}f\,d\mu_n=f(n)\to0\) for every \(f\in C_c(\mathbb R)\), so \(\mu_n\) converges vaguely to the zero measure. Thus vague convergence can lose total mass when tightness is absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dirac masses moving to infinity converge vaguely to zero but have no narrow probability limit, showing precisely how failure of tightness permits mass escape.
knowledge_statements.title: Mass-Escape Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The translating-Dirac example is mathematically correct and the failure-boundary kind is appropriate, but no inspectable source is cited.

children.title: Strongly Closed Admissible Classes

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Closed Admissible Classes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential characterization of strong closedness in metric spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space. An admissible class \(A\subset X\) is strongly closed if it is closed in the topology induced by \(d\). Equivalently, whenever \((x_n)\subset A\) and \(d(x_n,x)\to0\) for some \(x\in X\), one has \(x\in A\). In a normed space this criterion uses \(d(x,y)=\lVert x-y\rVert\). Hence strong closedness is sufficient to ensure that every strongly convergent minimizing subsequence in \(A\) has a feasible limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An admissible class is strongly closed when every norm- or metric-convergent sequence of feasible points has a feasible limit; this guarantees feasibility of strongly obtained limits.
assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space and \(A\subset X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is strongly closed exactly when \(x_n\in A\) and \(d(x_n,x)\to0\) imply \(x\in A\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: sequential closedness equals closedness in metric spaces

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space and \(A\subset X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is weakly sequentially closed exactly when \(x_n\in A\) and \(x_n\rightharpoonup x\) imply \(x\in A\).

notation.meaning: weak convergence in the Banach space
continuous dual of the Banach space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential weak closedness, the form used for minimizing sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Banach space. An admissible class \(A\subset X\) is weakly sequentially closed if every sequence \((x_n)\subset A\) satisfying \(x_n\rightharpoonup x\) has \(x\in A\), where weak convergence means \(x^*(x_n)\to x^*(x)\) for every \(x^*\in X^*\). If \(A\) is closed in the full weak topology, then it is weakly sequentially closed. The converse requires additional hypotheses and is not part of this definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A class is weakly sequentially closed when weak limits of feasible sequences remain feasible; full weak closedness always implies this sequential property.
knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Closed Admissible Classes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record correctly defines sequential weak closedness and distinguishes it from full weak closedness, but the terminology and distinction lack an inspectable citation.

$\forall l\in X^*$, there exists $x_l\in U(X)$ such that $l(x_l)=\sup_{x\in U(X)}l(x)$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: $U(X)$ is weakly compact, equivalently $X$ is reflexive.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\) is weak-star sequentially closed exactly when \(x_n\in A\) and \(x_n\overset{*}{\rightharpoonup}x\) imply \(x\in A\).

weak-star convergence induced by the predual

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential weak-star closedness relative to a fixed predual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=E^*\) be a dual Banach space with specified predual \(E\). An admissible class \(A\subset X\) is weak-star sequentially closed if \((x_n)\subset A\) and \(x_n\overset{*}{\rightharpoonup}x\) imply \(x\in A\), where weak-star convergence means \(\langle x_n,e\rangle\to\langle x,e\rangle\) for every \(e\in E\). Closure in the full weak-star topology implies this property; the converse generally needs metrizability or another sequentiality assumption on the relevant bounded set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative to a fixed predual, weak-star sequential closedness means every weak-star limit of a feasible sequence is feasible.

children.title: Closure-Topology Compatibility

assumptions_latex: \(A\subset X\), and the compactness argument produces convergence in a topology \(\tau\) on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Limit feasibility is guaranteed when \(A\) is \(\tau\)-sequentially closed; closure only in a strictly finer topology is insufficient in general.

notation.meaning: topology delivered by the compactness argument

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct-method feasibility requires closedness for the convergence topology actually obtained
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility condition between subsequential convergence and admissible-set closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a compactness argument yields \(x_{n_k}\to x\) in a topology \(\tau\) on \(X\), with \(x_{n_k}\in A\). The closure hypothesis compatible with that argument is \(\tau\)-sequential closedness of \(A\), namely \(x_{n_k}\in A\) and \(x_{n_k}\to x\) in \(\tau\) imply \(x\in A\). Closure in a topology strictly finer than \(\tau\) does not generally suffice. In particular, norm closedness alone need not preserve feasibility under weak or weak-star convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The admissible class must be closed for the topology in which compactness supplies a limit; closure only in a stronger topology may fail.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure-Topology Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The topology-compatibility condition is mathematically sound and fits the leaf, but it lacks cited support.

children.title: Constraint Preservation under Limits
children.top_down_role: Limit stability of pointwise, integral, differential, and boundary constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Preservation under Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract sequential criterion covering multiple constraint types.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,\tau)\) be a topological space, let \(I\) be an index set, and, for every \(i\in I\), let \(Y_i\) be a topological space, \(G_i:X\to Y_i\), and \(C_i\subset Y_i\) be sequentially closed. Assume that, for each \(i\in I\), whenever \(x_n\to x\) in \(\tau\) and \(G_i(x_n)\in C_i\) for all \(n\), one has \(G_i(x_n)\to G_i(x)\) in \(Y_i\). Then \(A=\bigcap_{i\in I}G_i^{-1}(C_i)\) is \(\tau\)-sequentially closed. Pointwise, integral, differential, and boundary constraints fit this principle once the corresponding limit-passage property is established.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A family of constraints is preserved under a chosen sequential limit when every defining quantity converges in its specified target topology and every allowed target set is sequentially closed.
assumptions_latex: \((X,\tau)\) is a topological space and \(I\) is an index set.
For every \(i\in I\), \(Y_i\) is a topological space, \(G_i:X\to Y_i\), and \(C_i\subset Y_i\) is sequentially closed.
For every \(i\in I\), if \(x_n\to x\) in \(\tau\) and \(G_i(x_n)\in C_i\) for all \(n\), then \(G_i(x_n)\to G_i(x)\) in \(Y_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible class \(A=\bigcap_{i\in I}G_i^{-1}(C_i)\) is \(\tau\)-sequentially closed.

notation.meaning: constraint maps into topological target spaces

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is strongly lower semicontinuous exactly when \(x_n\to x\) implies \(F(x)\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}F(x_n)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: sequential lower semicontinuity characterizes lower semicontinuity in metric spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential lower semicontinuity for the metric or norm topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space and let \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). The functional \(F\) is strongly lower semicontinuous if, for every sequence \((x_n)\subset X\) with \(d(x_n,x)\to0\), one has \(F(x)\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}F(x_n)\). Equivalently in a metric space, every sublevel set \(\{x\in X:F(x)\le c\}\) is strongly closed for each \(c\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A functional is strongly lower semicontinuous when its value at every metric limit does not exceed the limiting lower values along the sequence.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Lower Semicontinuity

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be Hausdorff and \(f:\mathcal X\to[-\infty,+\infty]\). The following are equivalent: \(\text{(i) }f\text{ is lower semicontinuous};\ \text{(ii) }\operatorname{epi}f\text{ is closed in }\mathcal X\times\mathbb R;\ \text{(iii) }(\forall\xi\in\mathbb R)\ \operatorname{lev}_{\leq\xi}f\text{ is closed in }\mathcal X.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower, Upper, and Two-Sided Semicontinuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real-valued functions on Hausdorff spaces, including the finite-valued domain of continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be Hausdorff, \(f:\mathcal X\to[-\infty,+\infty]\), and \(x\in\mathcal X\). The function \(f\) is lower semicontinuous at \(x\) iff every net \((x_a)_{a\in A}\) satisfies \(x_a\to x\Rightarrow f(x)\leq\liminf_a f(x_a)\); equivalently, for every \(\xi\in\mathbb R\) with \(\xi<f(x)\), some neighborhood \(V\) of \(x\) satisfies \(f(V)\subset(\xi,+\infty]\). It is lower semicontinuous iff this holds at every point. It is upper semicontinuous at \(x\) iff \(-f\) is lower semicontinuous there, equivalently \(x_a\to x\Rightarrow\limsup_a f(x_a)\leq f(x)\). If it is both lower and upper semicontinuous at \(x\), then every net converging to \(x\) has \(f(x_a)\to f(x)\). Finally, \(\operatorname{cont}f=\{x\in\mathcal X\mid f(x)\in\mathbb R\text{ and }f\text{ is continuous at }x\}\subset\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f\); continuity outside \(\operatorname{cont}f\) may still occur at points where \(f\) equals \(\pm\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an extended-real-valued function on a Hausdorff space, lower semicontinuity at a point means that its value does not exceed the lower limit along any convergent net; equivalently, every real level strictly below that value remains a strict lower bound throughout some neighborhood. Upper semicontinuity is lower semicontinuity of the negative function. Lower and upper semicontinuity together give continuity. The domain cont f consists only of finite-valued continuity points, lies in the interior of the effective domain, and does not include possible continuity points at infinite values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is lsc at }x\iff(\forall(x_a),\ x_a\to x\Rightarrow f(x)\leq\liminf_a f(x_a))\iff(\forall\xi<f(x))(\exists V\in\mathcal V(x))\ f(V)\subset(\xi,+\infty]\), with the stated upper-semicontinuity, continuity, and \(\operatorname{cont}f\) consequences.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weierstrass Attainment Theorem for Lower-Semicontinuous Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded general topological attainment result for extended-real-valued functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be a Hausdorff space, let \(f:\mathcal X\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) be lower semicontinuous, and let \(C\subseteq\mathcal X\) be compact with \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}f\neq\varnothing\). Then there exists \(\bar x\in C\) such that \(f(\bar x)=\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an extended-real-valued lower-semicontinuous function on a Hausdorff space has a compact feasible set meeting its effective domain, then it attains its infimum on that set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\bar x\in C:\ f(\bar x)=\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower Limits and Lower Semicontinuity in Euclidean Space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the lower limit through shrinking balls or neighborhoods and defines pointwise and global lower semicontinuity for extended-real-valued functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}} and \bar x\in\mathbb{R}^n,\quad \liminf_{x\to\bar x}f(x):=\lim_{\delta\searrow0}\inf_{x\in B(\bar x,\delta)}f(x)=\sup_{\delta>0}\inf_{x\in B(\bar x,\delta)}f(x)=\sup_{V\in\mathcal N(\bar x)}\inf_{x\in V}f(x). The function f is lower semicontinuous at \bar x iff \liminf_{x\to\bar x}f(x)\ge f(\bar x), equivalently iff equality holds; it is lower semicontinuous on \mathbb{R}^n iff this holds for every \bar x. Moreover, \liminf_{x\to\bar x}f(x)\le f(\bar x) always.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower limit at a point is the supremum of the infima of the function over neighborhoods shrinking to that point. A function is lower semicontinuous at the point when this lower limit is at least its value there, which is equivalent to equality because the lower limit never exceeds the point value. Global lower semicontinuity means this holds at every point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is lsc at }\bar x\iff \liminf_{x\to\bar x}f(x)=f(\bar x),\qquad f\text{ is lsc on }\mathbb{R}^n\iff \forall\bar x\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ \liminf_{x\to\bar x}f(x)=f(\bar x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower Semicontinuity under Continuous Pullback
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preservation of lower semicontinuity by precomposition with a continuous map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) and \(\mathcal Y\) be Hausdorff spaces, let \(T:\mathcal X\to\mathcal Y\) be continuous, and let \(g:\mathcal Y\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) be lower semicontinuous. Then \(f=g\circ T:\mathcal X\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) is lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Precomposing an extended-real-valued lower-semicontinuous function with a continuous map between Hausdorff spaces preserves lower semicontinuity.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\text{ and }\mathcal Y\text{ are Hausdorff spaces}\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Net Representation of the Lower Limit
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation of a function's topological lower limit at a point by convergent nets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be Hausdorff, let \(f:\mathcal X\to[-\infty,+\infty]\), let \(x\in\mathcal X\), and let \(\mathrm N(x)\) denote all nets in \(\mathcal X\) converging to \(x\). Then \[\liminf_{y\to x}f(y)=\min_{(x_a)_{a\in A}\in\mathrm N(x)}\liminf_a f(x_a).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an extended-real-valued function on a Hausdorff space, the lower limit at a point equals the minimum, over all nets converging to that point, of the lower limit of the function along the net.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle \liminf_{y\to x}f(y)=\min_{(x_a)_{a\in A}\in\mathrm N(x)}\liminf_a f(x_a)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Finite-Sum Closure of Lower Semicontinuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preservation under finite strictly positive linear combinations, with functions forbidden from taking the value minus infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be Hausdorff, let \((f_i)_{i\in I}\) be a finite family of lower semicontinuous functions \(f_i:\mathcal X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and let \(\alpha_i\in\mathbb R_{++}\) for every \(i\in I\). Then \(\sum_{i\in I}\alpha_i f_i\) is lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite strictly positive linear combination of lower-semicontinuous functions on a Hausdorff space is lower semicontinuous, provided the functions may take positive infinity but never negative infinity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed-Epigraph and Closed-Level-Set Characterization of Lower Semicontinuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes global lower semicontinuity of an arbitrary extended-real-valued function on Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}. The following are equivalent: (i) f is lower semicontinuous on \mathbb{R}^n; (ii) \operatorname{epi}f is closed in \mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}; (iii) \operatorname{lev}_{\le\alpha}f:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:f(x)\le\alpha\} is closed in \mathbb{R}^n for every \alpha\in\mathbb{R}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-real-valued function on Euclidean space is lower semicontinuous exactly when its epigraph is closed, and exactly when every real sublevel set is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is lsc}\iff \operatorname{epi}f\text{ is closed}\iff \forall\alpha\in\mathbb{R},\ \operatorname{lev}_{\le\alpha}f\text{ is closed}.

children.title: Weak Lower Semicontinuity
children.top_down_role: Lower-semicontinuity routes for weakly convergent sequences or nets.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is weakly sequentially lower semicontinuous exactly when \(x_n\rightharpoonup x\) implies \(F(x)\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}F(x_n)\).

notation.meaning: weak convergence in the Banach space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential weak lower semicontinuity used in the direct method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Banach space and let \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). The functional \(F\) is weakly sequentially lower semicontinuous if every weakly convergent sequence \(x_n\rightharpoonup x\) satisfies \(F(x)\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}F(x_n)\). Lower semicontinuity for the full weak topology implies this sequential property. Moreover, weak sequential lower semicontinuity implies strong sequential lower semicontinuity because norm convergence implies weak convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A functional is weakly sequentially lower semicontinuous when its value at a weak limit is no greater than the sequence's limiting lower values.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Lower Semicontinuity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sequential weak lower-semicontinuity definition and its distinction from full weak-topological lower semicontinuity are correct, but they lack an inspectable source.

children.title: Weak-Star Lower Semicontinuity

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space with dual \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is weak-star lower semicontinuous exactly when \(x_\alpha^*\overset{*}{\rightharpoonup}x^*\) implies \(F(x^*)\leq\liminf_\alpha F(x_\alpha^*)\).

notation.meaning: weak-star convergence in the dual space

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard net characterization of lower semicontinuity in the weak-star topology
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological, net-based definition; sequential formulations require additional metrizability or compactness hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The functional \(F\) is weak-star lower semicontinuous if every net \((x_\alpha^*)\subset X^*\) satisfying \(x_\alpha^*\overset{*}{\rightharpoonup}x^*\) obeys \[F(x^*)\leq\liminf_\alpha F(x_\alpha^*).\] Equivalently, each sublevel set \(\{x^*\in X^*:F(x^*)\leq c\}\) is closed in \(\sigma(X^*,X)\) for every \(c\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak-star lower semicontinuity means that functional values at weak-star limits do not exceed the liminf of values along convergent nets.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Star Lower Semicontinuity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The net and sublevel-set characterizations are mathematically appropriate for weak-star lower semicontinuity, and the definition content kind fits the leaf. No inspectable source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Topology-Compatibility Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Dependence of lower semicontinuity on the chosen convergence topology.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Norm continuity does not imply weak lower semicontinuity: \(e_n\rightharpoonup0\) but \(F(0)>\liminf_nF(e_n)\).

notation.meaning: the norm-continuous functional used in the counterexample

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit Hilbert-space counterexample separates norm continuity from weak lower semicontinuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete boundary between strong-topology continuity and weak-topology lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(F:\ell^2\to\mathbb R\) by \(F(x)=-\lVert x\rVert_2\). The functional is norm-continuous, while \(e_n\rightharpoonup0\) in \(\ell^2\) and \[F(0)=0> -1=\liminf_{n\to\infty}F(e_n).\] Thus lower semicontinuity in a stronger topology cannot be transferred automatically to a weaker topology; the chosen convergence topology must be compatible with the functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A norm-continuous functional may fail to be weakly lower semicontinuous, so the direct method must use lower semicontinuity in the compactness topology.
knowledge_statements.title: Topology-Compatibility Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The explicit ell^2 example correctly separates norm continuity from weak lower semicontinuity, and failure_boundary fits the topology-compatibility leaf. A specific authoritative source locator is absent.

children.title: Convex Integral-Functional Lower Semicontinuity
children.top_down_role: Convexity-based lower-semicontinuity for variational integrals.

assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) is measurable with finite measure and \(1<p<\infty\).
\(f:\Omega\times\mathbb R^m\to[0,+\infty]\) is measurable in \(x\), lower semicontinuous and convex in \(z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(u_n\rightharpoonup u\) in \(L^p(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\), then \(I(u)\leq\liminf_n I(u_n)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard weak lower-semicontinuity theorem for nonnegative convex normal integrands
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonnegative convex normal-integrand version on reflexive Lebesgue spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\), set \[I(u)=\int_\Omega f(x,u(x))\,dx,\] with the integral allowed to equal \(+\infty\). Then \(I\) is sequentially weakly lower semicontinuous on \(L^p(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\): whenever \(u_n\rightharpoonup u\), \[I(u)\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}I(u_n).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integrating a nonnegative lower-semicontinuous convex integrand produces a weakly lower-semicontinuous functional on a reflexive Lebesgue space.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Integral-Functional Lower Semicontinuity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem is a standard convex-integral lower-semicontinuity result, but no source certifies that the stated measurability and lower-semicontinuity assumptions are sufficient in precisely this formulation. The theorem content kind fits the leaf.

children.top_down_role: Weak lower-semicontinuity regimes based on polyconvex structure.

convex representative of the polyconvex density

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Autonomous first-order integrals; polyconvexity is used as a sufficient condition for quasiconvexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Polyconvexity means that there is a convex function \(g\) on the finite-dimensional space of minors such that \(f(A)=g(M(A))\) for every \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}\). Such an \(f\) is quasiconvex. Consequently, if \(u_n\rightharpoonup u\) in \(W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\), then \[\int_\Omega f(\nabla u)\,dx\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega f(\nabla u_n)\,dx.\]

children.title: Vectorial Integral Regimes
children.top_down_role: Dimension-sensitive settings for vector-valued variational integrals.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^{m\times d}\to\mathbb R\) is a Borel density for a first-order autonomous integral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The vectorial weak lower-semicontinuity condition is Morrey quasiconvexity; when \(m=1\) or \(d=1\), it reduces to ordinary convexity.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: Morrey quasiconvexity is the local gradient-variation condition governing vectorial first-order integrals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes genuinely vectorial problems from scalar or one-dimensional regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The relevant vectorial condition is \[f(A)\leq\frac1{|Q|}\int_Q f(A+\nabla\varphi(y))\,dy\] for every \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}\) and every \(\varphi\in W^{1,\infty}_0(Q;\mathbb R^m)\). For scalar-valued maps \(m=1\), or for one-dimensional domains \(d=1\), this condition is equivalent to convexity of \(f\). When \(m,d\geq2\), it is generally strictly weaker than convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vectorial gradient integrals are governed by quasiconvexity; only scalar-valued or one-dimensional regimes collapse this condition to ordinary convexity.
knowledge_statements.title: Vectorial Integral Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quasiconvexity formula and its reduction to convexity when m=1 or d=1 fit the regime leaf. children.title: Convexity-Gap Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Separations among convexity notions relevant to lower semicontinuity.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Rank-one convexity is strictly weaker than quasiconvexity and therefore cannot alone guarantee weak lower semicontinuity of vectorial integral functionals.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical multidimensional counterexamples separate rank-one convexity from quasiconvexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical multidimensional separation; the exact counterexample and hypotheses require source certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists a finite-valued function \(f:\mathbb R^{3\times2}\to\mathbb R\) whose restriction \(t\mapsto f(A+t(a\otimes b))\) is convex for every \(A\), \(a\), and \(b\), but for which some cube \(Q\), matrix \(A\), and \(\varphi\in W^{1,\infty}_0(Q;\mathbb R^3)\) satisfy \[f(A)>\frac1{|Q|}\int_Q f(A+\nabla\varphi(y))\,dy.\] Thus rank-one convexity does not imply quasiconvexity in general.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In genuinely vectorial dimensions, rank-one convexity need not imply quasiconvexity, so it is insufficient by itself for weak lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity-Gap Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed 3-by-2 separation of rank-one convexity from quasiconvexity is a specialized counterexample and cannot be certified by standard-field rationale alone. The failure_boundary content kind is appropriate, but an exact source and locator are required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-Order Expansion of a Perturbed Nonsingular Minimum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local sensitivity of a nonsingular minimum under an additive smooth perturbation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Distance Penalization Theorem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global exact penalization of a metric-space constraint by distance to the feasible set, including the strict-penalty converse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(X,m)$ be a metric space, let $\varnothing\ne C\subset X$, and let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be Lipschitz on $X$ with constant $K\ge0$. Define $d_C(x):=\inf_{y\in C}m(x,y)$. If $\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)$, then for every $\widehat K\ge K$, $\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\bigl(f(x)+\widehat Kd_C(x)\bigr)$. Conversely, if $C$ is closed and $\widehat K>K$, every global minimizer of $f+\widehat Kd_C$ over $X$ belongs to $C$ and minimizes $f$ over $C$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constrained global minimizer of a K-Lipschitz function also minimizes the distance-penalized objective when the penalty coefficient is at least K. If the feasible set is closed and the coefficient is strictly greater than K, every global penalized minimizer is feasible and solves the constrained problem.
assumptions_latex: $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is globally Lipschitz with constant $K\ge0$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat K\ge K\Rightarrow \bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\bigl(f(x)+\widehat Kd_C(x)\bigr);\quad C\text{ closed},\ \widehat K>K\Rightarrow\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}(f(x)+\widehat Kd_C(x))\subseteq\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convergence of Minimizing Sequences for Coercive Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak cluster-point optimality and strictness-dependent weak or strong convergence for coercive closed proper convex functions on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\Gamma_0(\mathcal H)\) be coercive and let \((x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\) be a minimizing sequence of \(f\). Then: (i) \((x_n)\) has a weak sequential cluster point and every such point minimizes \(f\); (ii) if \(f\) is strictly convex, then \(f\) has a unique minimizer \(x\) and \(x_n\rightharpoonup x\); (iii) if \(f\) is uniformly convex on every nonempty bounded subset of \(\operatorname{dom}f\), then \(f\) has a unique minimizer \(x\) and \(x_n\to x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a coercive proper lower-semicontinuous convex function, every minimizing sequence has weak cluster points and all are minimizers. Strict convexity gives uniqueness and weak convergence; uniform convexity on every nonempty bounded subset of the domain gives uniqueness and strong convergence.
assumptions_latex: \((x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\) is a minimizing sequence of \(f\).
For conclusion (iii), \(f\) is uniformly convex on every nonempty bounded subset of \(\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every weak sequential cluster point of \((x_n)\) lies in \(\operatorname{Argmin}f\); under strict convexity, \(\operatorname{Argmin}f=\{x\}\) and \(x_n\rightharpoonup x\); under the stated uniform-convexity condition, \(\operatorname{Argmin}f=\{x\}\) and \(x_n\to x\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit loss of attainment caused by minimizers escaping to infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Each \(F_n\) is continuous and coercive, hence has a unique minimizer \(x_n<0\) determined by \(e^{x_n}+2x_n/n=0\). The convergence \(F_n\to F\) is locally uniform and therefore implies Gamma-convergence on \(\mathbb R\). Nevertheless, \(x_n\to-\infty\), \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R}F_n(x)\to0=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}F(x),\] and \(F(x)>0\) for every finite \(x\). Thus \(F\) does not attain its infimum, and \((F_n)\) is not equi-coercive.

children.title: Escape to Infinity
children.top_down_role: Loss of compactness through unbounded minimizing sequences.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric-space form of nonattainment caused by failure of boundedness or coercivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(x_0\in X\). Escape to infinity occurs when a minimizing sequence \((x_n)\) satisfies \(d(x_n,x_0)\to\infty\); more generally, it occurs when \((x_n)\) eventually leaves every compact subset of \(X\). Consequently, \((x_n)\) has no convergent subsequence and the direct compactness argument cannot produce a minimizer. In a proper metric space, the condition \(d(x_n,x_0)\to\infty\) is equivalent to eventual escape from every compact set. A sufficient boundary mechanism is failure of inf-compactness: some sublevel set \(S_\alpha\) containing a minimizing tail is noncompact and admits such an escaping sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimizing sequence escapes to infinity when it leaves every compact set, preventing extraction of a convergent subsequence and hence compactness-based attainment.
knowledge_statements.title: Escape to Infinity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but no citation supports the proper-space equivalence or the stated inf-compactness mechanism.

Thus the topology supplies a limit, yet feasibility is not preserved. Even if an extension \(\widetilde F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is lower semicontinuous and satisfies \(\widetilde F(x)\leq\liminf_n F(x_n)=m\), the point \(x\) cannot attain the original problem over \(C\). Replacing \(C\) by \(\overline C\) defines a relaxation and may lower the optimal value unless every newly feasible limit has value at least \(m\).

Hence \(x\) need not minimize \(F\), and the direct method fails at the lower-semicontinuity step. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Characterizations of the Lower-Semicontinuous Envelope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded properties of the lower-semicontinuous envelope on a Hausdorff space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be Hausdorff, let \(f:\mathcal X\to[-\infty,+\infty]\), and let \(\bar f\) be its lower-semicontinuous envelope. Then: (i) \(\bar f\) is the greatest lower-semicontinuous function satisfying \(\bar f\leq f\); (ii) \(\operatorname{epi}\bar f\) is closed; (iii) \(\operatorname{dom}f\subseteq\operatorname{dom}\bar f\subseteq\overline{\operatorname{dom}f}\); (iv) \((\forall x\in\mathcal X)\ \bar f(x)=\liminf_{y\to x}f(y)\); (v) for every \(x\in\mathcal X\), \(f\) is lower semicontinuous at \(x\) if and only if \(\bar f(x)=f(x)\); and (vi) \(\operatorname{epi}\bar f=\overline{\operatorname{epi}f}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower-semicontinuous envelope is the greatest lower-semicontinuous minorant of the function. Its epigraph is the closure of the original epigraph, its domain lies between the original domain and its closure, its values are the pointwise lower limits, and equality with the original function at a point is equivalent to lower semicontinuity there.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar f\text{ is the lower-semicontinuous envelope of }f\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar f=\max\{g\leq f:g\text{ is lower semicontinuous}\},\quad \operatorname{epi}\bar f=\overline{\operatorname{epi}f},\quad \operatorname{dom}f\subseteq\operatorname{dom}\bar f\subseteq\overline{\operatorname{dom}f},\quad \bar f(x)=\liminf_{y\to x}f(y),\quad [f\text{ is lsc at }x\iff\bar f(x)=f(x)]\)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(u_n(x)=a(nx)\) for \(x\in Q\). Periodic averaging gives \(u_n\rightharpoonup0\) in \(L^p(Q)\), while \(\|u_n\|_{L^p(Q)}\to\|a\|_{L^p(Y)}>0\). children.title: Lower-Semicontinuous Envelopes
children.top_down_role: Topological closure of objective models.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline F\) is the greatest lower-semicontinuous function satisfying \(\overline F\leq F\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological lower-semicontinuous minorant envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The lower-semicontinuous envelope of \(F\) is defined by
\[\overline F(x)=\sup_{U\in\mathcal N(x)}\inf_{y\in U}F(y).\]
It satisfies \(\overline F\leq F\), is lower semicontinuous, and dominates every lower-semicontinuous function \(G:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) with \(G\leq F\). If \(X\) is first countable, then
\[\overline F(x)=\inf\left\{\liminf_{n\to\infty}F(x_n):x_n\to x\right\}.\]
Thus minimizing the envelope is the canonical relaxation associated with the chosen topology; changing that topology can change the envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower-semicontinuous envelope is the greatest lower-semicontinuous minorant of an objective and admits a neighborhood, or sequential, relaxation formula.
knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Semicontinuous Envelopes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits, but the neighborhood and first-countable sequential formulas need a citation; the envelope may take minus infinity unless additional boundedness is imposed or its codomain is enlarged.

children.title: Convex Envelopes
children.top_down_role: Convex relaxation for scalar or finite-dimensional nonconvex models.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and bounded below by an affine function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^{**}\) is the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex minorant of \(f\).
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional lower-semicontinuous convex envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The lower-semicontinuous convex envelope of \(f\) is its Fenchel biconjugate
\[f^{**}(x)=\sup_{z\in\mathbb R^m}\{\langle z,x\rangle-f^*(z)\}.\]
It is convex and lower semicontinuous, satisfies \(f^{**}\leq f\), and dominates every lower-semicontinuous convex function \(g\) with \(g\leq f\). Equivalently,
\[f^{**}(x)=\inf\left\{\liminf_{n\to\infty}\sum_{i=1}^{k_n}\lambda_{n,i}f(x_{n,i}):\sum_i\lambda_{n,i}x_{n,i}\to x,\ \lambda_{n,i}\geq0,\ \sum_i\lambda_{n,i}=1\right\}.\]
If \(f\) is already lower semicontinuous and convex, then \(f^{**}=f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Fenchel biconjugate is the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex function below the original integrand.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Envelopes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits, but both the Fenchel–Moreau characterization and the stated sequential barycentric formula require an inspectable source.

children.title: Quasiconvex Envelopes
children.top_down_role: Relaxation adapted to vectorial gradient structures.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^{m\times d}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is Borel measurable and bounded below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Qf\) is the greatest quasiconvex minorant of \(f\) under the stated cell-formula hypotheses.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Morrey quasiconvex envelope for first-order gradient integrands.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A function \(g:\mathbb R^{m\times d}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is quasiconvex when, for every \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times d}\) and \(\phi\in W_0^{1,\infty}(Y;\mathbb R^m)\),
\[g(A)\leq\int_Y g(A+\nabla\phi(y))\,dy.\]
The quasiconvex envelope is
\[Qf(A)=\sup\{g(A):g\leq f,\ g\text{ is quasiconvex}\}.\]
Under standard continuity and growth assumptions ensuring the cell representation, it is equivalently given by the appropriate relaxed cell formula obtained by infimizing \(\int_Y f(A+\nabla\phi)\,dy\) over zero-boundary microscopic perturbations, with multicell relaxation when required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The quasiconvex envelope is the greatest quasiconvex minorant and, under suitable growth and continuity assumptions, has a microscopic cell representation.
knowledge_statements.title: Quasiconvex Envelopes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits, but the assumptions do not specify the continuity and growth hypotheses under which the one-cell or multicell formula is valid.

children.title: Envelope Selection Regimes
children.top_down_role: Model features determining the appropriate geometric envelope.

assumptions_latex: The relaxation topology and admissible microscopic perturbations are fixed before taking the envelope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The correct envelope is selected by the convergence mode and differential constraints, not by the integrand alone.

notation.meaning: Convex envelope of a zero-order integrand.
Quasiconvex envelope of a gradient integrand.

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection rule for common relaxation envelopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an objective \(F\), relaxation first selects the greatest minorant that is lower semicontinuous in the prescribed topology \(\tau\), namely \(\operatorname{cl}_{\tau}F\). For zero-order integral functionals under weak convergence, unrestricted mixing of values typically selects the lower-semicontinuous convex envelope \(f^{**}\). For first-order functionals \(F(u)=\int_\Omega f(\nabla u(x))\,dx\) under weak Sobolev convergence, gradient compatibility restricts microscopic mixtures and typically selects the lower-semicontinuous quasiconvex envelope \(Qf\). Additional differential constraints may require corresponding constrained convexity notions. Therefore envelope choice is determined jointly by topology, locality, and admissible perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak zero-order mixing generally selects convexification, whereas weak gradient relaxation selects quasiconvexification; topology and differential constraints govern the choice.
knowledge_statements.title: Envelope Selection Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind fits, but the convexification and quasiconvexification regimes are stated too generally without functional, topology, growth, and admissibility hypotheses or supporting citations.

children.title: Envelope-Gap Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Differences between original energies and their relaxed envelopes.

assumptions_latex: \(E f\) is the envelope selected by the topology and admissible perturbations, with \(Ef\leq f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pointwise envelope gap is nonzero exactly where \(Ef<f\); an optimization-value gap additionally requires access to that region.
review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes pointwise envelope gaps from gaps in optimal values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\Delta_f(x)=f(x)-Ef(x)\in[0,+\infty]\). The envelope is exact at \(x\) precisely when \(\Delta_f(x)=0\), and a pointwise relaxation gap occurs precisely when \(Ef(x)<f(x)\). For a variational problem with original infimum \(m\) and relaxed infimum \(\overline m\), one always has \(\overline m\leq m\). A strict value gap \(\overline m<m\) can occur only when admissible relaxed competitors exploit states or microstructures where the selected envelope is strictly below the original density. Conversely, a pointwise gap need not change the infimum if every minimizing competitor avoids the gap region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An envelope differs from the original function exactly on its pointwise gap set, but the optimal value changes only when admissible competitors exploit that set.
knowledge_statements.title: Envelope-Gap Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, but f-Ef is undefined where both values are positive infinity, and the asserted necessary mechanism for a strict value gap needs a precise formulation and source.

children.title: Measure-Valued Generalized Minimizers
children.top_down_role: Generalized minimizing objects represented through measures.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\) is a nonempty admissible set in a Hausdorff state space \(Z\).
\(F:Z\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is Borel measurable and bounded below on \(\mathcal A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle \int_Z F(z)\,d\mu^*(z)=\inf_{\mu\in\mathcal P(\mathcal A)}\int_Z F(z)\,d\mu(z)\).

notation.meaning: Borel probability measures supported on the admissible set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probability-measure relaxation on an admissible state space; the intended relation to Young measures requires source confirmation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A measure-valued generalized minimizer of \(F\) over \(\mathcal A\) is a probability measure \(\mu^*\in\mathcal P(\mathcal A)\) for which \(F\) is \(\mu^*\)-integrable and
\[
\int_Z F(z)\,d\mu^*(z)=\inf_{\mu\in\mathcal P(\mathcal A)}\int_Z F(z)\,d\mu(z).
\]
If additional constraints are expressed through moments or barycenters, \(\mathcal P(\mathcal A)\) is replaced by the corresponding weakly closed subset of probability measures satisfying those constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A measure-valued minimizer is an admissible probability distribution attaining the least expected energy, with any prescribed moment or barycenter constraints imposed on the distribution.
knowledge_statements.title: Measure-Valued Generalized Minimizers

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports this probability-measure relaxation or its intended relation to Young measures. The unconstrained formulation also reduces to randomization over ordinary admissible states, so its status as a generalized-minimizer representation depends on the intended convention.

children.title: Parametrized Generalized Minimizers
children.top_down_role: Spatially indexed generalized limits for fine-scale behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) is measurable with finite measure.
\(f:\Omega\times\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is a normal integrand bounded below by an integrable function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(\displaystyle \mathcal I(
u^*)=\inf_{
u\in\mathcal Y}\int_\Omega\int_{\mathbb R^m}f(x,\xi)\,d
u_x(\xi)\,dx\).

notation.meaning: admissible class of weakly measurable probability kernels
probability measure assigned to the parameter point x

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Young-measure interpretation with the physical variable as parameter; admissibility may include barycentric or differential constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A parametrized generalized minimizer is a weakly measurable family \(\nu^*=\{\nu_x^*\}_{x\in\Omega}\) of Borel probability measures on \(\mathbb R^m\), belonging to a specified admissible class \(\mathcal Y\), such that
\[
\mathcal I(\nu^*):=\int_\Omega\int_{\mathbb R^m}f(x,\xi)\,d\nu_x^*(\xi)\,dx
=
\inf_{\nu\in\mathcal Y}\int_\Omega\int_{\mathbb R^m}f(x,\xi)\,d\nu_x(\xi)\,dx.
\]
Any pointwise, barycentric, or differential constraint defining the relaxation is included in \(\mathcal Y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parametrized generalized minimizer is a measurable probability kernel that satisfies the relaxed constraints and minimizes the energy obtained by averaging the integrand at each parameter point.
knowledge_statements.title: Parametrized Generalized Minimizers

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Young-measure formulation is plausible and the representation content kind fits, but the admissible kernel class and any barycentric or differential constraints are essential to the mathematical meaning and require an authoritative source.

children.title: Oscillation Representation
children.top_down_role: Generalized limit objects capturing unresolved oscillatory structure.

assumptions_latex: \(1\le p<\infty\) and \((u_j)\) is bounded in \(L^p(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\).
\(g:\Omega\times\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\) is Carathéodory and \((g(\cdot,u_j))\) is uniformly integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle g(\cdot,u_j)\rightharpoonup \bigl[x\mapsto\int g(x,\xi)\,d\nu_x(\xi)\bigr]\) weakly in \(L^1(\Omega)\) along a subsequence.

notation.meaning: Young measure generated by a subsequence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical Young-measure representation of oscillation for an equiintegrable composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exist a subsequence, not relabeled, and a weakly measurable family \((\nu_x)_{x\in\Omega}\) of Borel probability measures on \(\mathbb R^m\) such that, for every Carathéodory integrand \(g\) whose compositions \((g(\cdot,u_j))\) are uniformly integrable,
\[
g(\cdot,u_j)\rightharpoonup \left[x\mapsto\int_{\mathbb R^m}g(x,\xi)\,d\nu_x(\xi)\right]
\quad\text{weakly in }L^1(\Omega).
\]
Thus \(\nu_x\) records the limiting distribution of bounded-scale oscillations at almost every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded sequence has a subsequence whose nonlinear, uniformly integrable observations converge to averages against a pointwise probability measure describing its oscillations.
knowledge_statements.title: Oscillation Representation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a standard Young-measure oscillation representation and the content kind fits, but no citation is supplied for the subsequence theorem, measurability conditions, or uniformly integrable composition conclusion.

children.title: Concentration Representation
children.top_down_role: Generalized limit objects retaining concentrated mass or energy.

assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d\) is bounded and \((u_j)\) is bounded in \(L^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^m)\).
\(f\) is continuous with linear growth and has a continuous recession function \(f^\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle f(u_j)\,dx\stackrel{*}{\rightharpoonup}\langle f,\nu_x\rangle\,dx+\langle f^\infty,\nu_x^\infty\rangle\,d\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized Young-measure representation for linear-growth integrands and concentration at infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
After passage to a subsequence, there are a Young measure \((\nu_x)\), a finite positive measure \(\lambda\) on \(\overline\Omega\), and a \(\lambda\)-measurable family \((\nu_x^\infty)\) of probability measures on the unit sphere such that
\[
f(u_j)\,dx\stackrel{*}{\rightharpoonup}
\left(\int_{\mathbb R^m}f(\xi)\,d\nu_x(\xi)\right)dx+
\left(\int_{\mathbb S^{m-1}}f^\infty(\theta)\,d\nu_x^\infty(\theta)\right)d\lambda
\]
as finite Radon measures. The second term represents concentration magnitude and direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized Young measure separates nonlinear limits into an oscillation average and a singular term encoding the magnitude and directions of concentration.
knowledge_statements.title: Concentration Representation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The oscillation–concentration decomposition is plausible, but the precise generalized Young-measure convention, domain of the concentration measure, recession-function hypotheses, and measure convergence require source confirmation.
