knowledge_statements.statement_title: Characterizations and Consequences of Directional Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent criteria, an implication from ordinary Robinson constraint qualification, and a characterization of parameter-relative feasible directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At \(x_0\in\Phi(u_0)\) and in direction \(d\), directional regularity is equivalent to each of
\[0\in\operatorname{int}\bigl(G(x_0,u_0)+DG(x_0,u_0)(X,\mathbb R_+d)-K\bigr)\]
and the existence of \(\delta,\varepsilon>0\) such that
\[\varepsilon B_Y\subset G(x_0,u_0)+DG(x_0,u_0)(B_X,\delta d)-K.\]
Robinson's constraint qualification implies directional regularity for every direction \(d\). If directional regularity holds in direction \(d\), then \(h\in X\) is a first-order feasible direction relative to \(d\) if and only if it satisfies condition (4.10).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directional regularity is equivalent to both the stated interior condition and the stated uniform ball inclusion. Ordinary Robinson constraint qualification implies directional regularity in every direction. Under directional regularity, the parameter-relative first-order feasible directions are exactly those satisfying the referenced linearized condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{DReg}(x_0;d)\iff 0\in\operatorname{int}\bigl(G(x_0,u_0)+DG(x_0,u_0)(X,\mathbb R_+d)-K\bigr)\iff\exists\delta,\varepsilon>0:\ \varepsilon B_Y\subset G(x_0,u_0)+DG(x_0,u_0)(B_X,\delta d)-K;\quad \operatorname{RCQ}(x_0,u_0)\Rightarrow\forall d\,\operatorname{DReg}(x_0;d);\quad \operatorname{DReg}(x_0;d)\Rightarrow\bigl[h\text{ is first-order feasible relative to }d\iff h\text{ satisfies (4.10)}\bigr].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-Order Expansion of Near-Optimal Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parametric equality and finitely constrained inequality problems under strict Robinson qualification and second-order conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(P_u)$ have equality constraints and finitely many inequality constraints. Let $\bar x(u)$ be an $\varepsilon(u)$-optimal solution converging to $x_0\in\mathcal S(u_0)$, with $\varepsilon(u)=o(\|u-u_0\|^2)$. Assume: (i) $f(\cdot,u)$ and $G(\cdot,u)$ are twice continuously differentiable, $D_{xx}^2f(x,u)$ and $D_{xx}^2G(x,u)$ are continuous at $(x_0,u_0)$, and $f(x_0,\cdot)$, $D_xf(x_0,\cdot)$, $G(x_0,\cdot)$, and $D_xG(x_0,\cdot)$ are locally Lipschitz near $u_0$; (ii) Robinson's constraint qualification with respect to the reduced cone $K_0$ holds; and (iii) the stated second-order conditions hold. If $\bar h(u)$ is the optimal solution of the associated auxiliary problem $(F_u)$, then $\|\bar x(u)-x_0-\bar h(u)\|=o(\|u-u_0\|)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smooth parametric problem with equality and finitely many inequality constraints, strict Robinson qualification and the stated second-order conditions make the auxiliary problem's optimizer a first-order approximation of every sufficiently accurate convergent near-optimal solution branch.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local error bound under Robinson constraint qualification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local residual-to-feasibility stability for a parameterized constraint system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_0\in\Phi(u_0)\), and suppose Robinson's constraint qualification holds at \((x_0,u_0)\). Then, for all \((x,u)\) sufficiently near \((x_0,u_0)\),
\[
\operatorname{dist}(x,\Phi(u))=O\!\left(\operatorname{dist}(G(x,u),K)\right).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If x0 is feasible at u0 and Robinson's constraint qualification holds there, then locally the distance to the parameterized feasible set is bounded by a constant multiple of the constraint residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dist}(x,\Phi(u))=O\!\left(\operatorname{dist}(G(x,u),K)\right)\quad\text{for }(x,u)\text{ near }(x_0,u_0).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero-direction optimality in tangent and linearized problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The feasible set is denoted by \(\Phi\), with constraint components \(Q\) and \(K\) as in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_0\) be a local solution of \((P)\), and suppose \(f\) and \(G\) are continuously differentiable at \(x_0\). Then \(h=0\) minimizes \(Df(x_0)h\) over \(h\in T_\Phi(x_0)\). If Robinson's constraint qualification \((3.13)\) also holds, then \(h=0\) minimizes \(Df(x_0)h\) subject to \(h\in T_Q(x_0)\) and \(DG(x_0)h\in T_K(G(x_0))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a differentiable local minimizer, the zero direction solves the objective's first-order minimization problem on the feasible tangent cone. Under Robinson qualification, it also solves the corresponding constraint-linearized problem.
assumptions_latex: x_0\text{ is a local optimal solution of }(P)
f\text{ and }G\text{ are continuously differentiable at }x_0
\text{For the linearized conclusion: Robinson CQ }(3.13)\text{ holds}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: 0\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{h\in T_\Phi(x_0)}Df(x_0)h,\qquad \text{and under Robinson CQ, }0\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\substack{h\in T_Q(x_0)\\DG(x_0)h\in T_K(G(x_0))}}Df(x_0)h

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict complementarity and consequences of nondegeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict complementarity and multiplier consequences for a feasible reducible constraint system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a feasible point $x_0$, with $y_0=G(x_0)$, strict complementarity holds if there exists $\lambda\in\Lambda(x_0)\cap\operatorname{ri}N_K(y_0)$. Nondegeneracy implies $DG(x_0)X+T_K(y_0)=Y$, which, when $Y$ is finite dimensional, is equivalent to Robinson's constraint qualification. Consequently, a nondegenerate local optimum admits a first-order Lagrange multiplier, and the corresponding multiplier is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict complementarity means that some Lagrange multiplier lies in the relative interior of the normal cone. Nondegeneracy is stronger than Robinson's constraint qualification and, at a local optimum, guarantees existence and uniqueness of the multiplier.
assumptions_latex: Y\text{ is finite dimensional for the equivalence with Robinson's constraint qualification}
x_0\text{ is a nondegenerate local optimum for the multiplier conclusions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Strict complementarity}\iff \Lambda(x_0)\cap\operatorname{ri}N_K(y_0)\ne\varnothing;\quad \text{nondegeneracy}\Rightarrow\text{Robinson CQ and a unique Lagrange multiplier at a local optimum}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Core and radial-cone characterizations of Robinson constraint qualification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent algebraic-core and radial-cone formulations of Robinson constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(G(x_0)\in K\). Then Robinson's constraint qualification at \(x_0\) is equivalent to each of
\[
0\in\operatorname{core}\bigl(G(x_0)+DG(x_0)X-K\bigr)
\]
and
\[
DG(x_0)X-\mathcal R_K(G(x_0))=Y.
\]
Thus these two conditions are also equivalent to each other.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a feasible point, Robinson's constraint qualification is equivalent both to an algebraic-core condition for the linearized displacement set and to surjectivity of the derivative range after subtracting the radial cone of K.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Robinson CQ at }x_0\iff 0\in\operatorname{core}\bigl(G(x_0)+DG(x_0)X-K\bigr)\iff DG(x_0)X-\mathcal R_K(G(x_0))=Y.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Automatic Relative-Interior Regimes for Robinson Qualification Equivalences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite-dimensional codomain or a constraint set with nonempty interior makes the usual Robinson qualification formulations equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal A:=DG(x_0)X-\mathcal R_K(G(x_0))\). If either \(\dim Y<\infty\) or \(\operatorname{int}K\neq\varnothing\), then \(\operatorname{ri}\mathcal A\neq\varnothing\). Consequently, Robinson's constraint qualification is equivalent to conditions
\[
DG(x_0)X-T_K(G(x_0))=Y,
\]
\[
[DG(x_0)X]^\perp\cap N_K(G(x_0))=\{0\},
\]
\[
\operatorname{cl}[DG(x_0)X-T_K(G(x_0))]=Y,
\quad
\operatorname{cl}[DG(x_0)X-\mathcal R_K(G(x_0))]=Y.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the codomain is finite dimensional or the constraint set has nonempty interior, the radial-cone difference set has nonempty relative interior. Robinson constraint qualification is then equivalent to the tangent-cone surjectivity, dual normal-cone, and two closure-density conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{ri}\mathcal A\neq\varnothing\quad\text{and}\quad \mathrm{RCQ}\Longleftrightarrow(2.182)\Longleftrightarrow(2.183)\Longleftrightarrow(2.184)\Longleftrightarrow(2.185).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nearby Approximate KKT Certificate for an \(\varepsilon\)-Optimal Solution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robinson's constraint qualification is required at every point of the closed radius-\(\sqrt\varepsilon\) ball around the given approximate solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varepsilon\geq0\). Suppose \(\bar x\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-optimal solution of \((P)\), \(f\) and \(G\) are continuously differentiable, and Robinson's constraint qualification holds at every \(x\in\overline B(\bar x,\sqrt\varepsilon)\). Then there exist an \(\varepsilon\)-optimal solution \(\widehat x\) of \((P)\) and \(\lambda\in Y^*\) such that \(\|\bar x-\widehat x\|\leq\sqrt\varepsilon\), \(\operatorname{dist}(-D_xL(\widehat x,\lambda),N_Q(\widehat x))\leq\sqrt\varepsilon\), and \(\lambda\in N_K(G(\widehat x))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an epsilon-optimal solution has continuously differentiable data and Robinson's constraint qualification holds throughout its closed radius-sqrt(epsilon) neighborhood, then there is a nearby epsilon-optimal solution with a multiplier whose stationarity residual is at most sqrt(epsilon) and which satisfies the constraint normal-cone condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\widehat x\in X,\ \exists\lambda\in Y^*:\ \widehat x\text{ is }\varepsilon\text{-optimal},\ \|\bar x-\widehat x\|\leq\sqrt\varepsilon,\ \operatorname{dist}(-D_xL(\widehat x,\lambda),N_Q(\widehat x))\leq\sqrt\varepsilon,\ \lambda\in N_K(G(\widehat x)).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tangent-cone formula under Robinson constraint qualification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coincidence and linearized representation of tangent-cone variants for a smooth inverse-image feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G:X\to Y\) be continuously differentiable at \(x_0\in\Phi:=G^{-1}(K)\), and suppose Robinson's constraint qualification holds. Then the inner, contingent, and Clarke tangent cones to \(\Phi\) at \(x_0\) coincide, and their common value is
\[
T_\Phi(x_0)=\{h\in X:DG(x_0)h\in T_K(G(x_0))\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under Robinson's constraint qualification, the inner, contingent, and Clarke tangent cones of the feasible set coincide and equal the cone obtained by linearizing G into the tangent cone of K.
assumptions_latex: G:X\to Y\text{ is continuously differentiable at }x_0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The inner, contingent, and Clarke tangent cones to }\Phi\text{ at }x_0\text{ coincide, and }T_\Phi(x_0)=\{h\in X:DG(x_0)h\in T_K(G(x_0))\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is metrically regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\), and a constant \(\kappa\geq 0\), such that
\[
d(x,F^{-1}(y))\leq \kappa\,d(y,F(x))\qquad\text{for every }(x,y)\in U\times V.
\]
The infimum of all admissible \(\kappa\) is the exact regularity modulus \(\operatorname{reg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric regularity bounds the distance to every nearby inverse image by the corresponding mapping residual, uniformly in both the decision and perturbation variables.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequentially Bounded Constraint Qualification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded multiplier selections along convergent sequences of variational-inequality solutions and the resulting local multiplier existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $x\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)$. SBCQ holds at $x$ if, for every sequence $\{x^k\}\subset\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)$ with $x^k\to x$, there exist an integer $\bar k>0$ and multiplier pairs $(\mu^k,\lambda^k)\in\mathcal M(x^k)$ for all $k\ge\bar k$ such that the selected sequence $\{(\mu^k,\lambda^k)\}_{k\ge\bar k}$ is bounded. SBCQ implies that $\mathcal M(x')\ne\varnothing$ for every $x'\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F)$ sufficiently close to $x$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: SBCQ requires a bounded choice of multipliers along every sequence of VI solutions converging to the reference solution. It guarantees that every sufficiently nearby solution has at least one multiplier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall\{x^k\}\to x\ \exists\bar k\ \exists\{(\mu^k,\lambda^k)\}_{k\ge\bar k}\text{ bounded with }(\mu^k,\lambda^k)\in\mathcal M(x^k);\quad \operatorname{SBCQ}(x)\Rightarrow\mathcal M(x')\ne\varnothing\text{ for all sufficiently nearby }x'\in\operatorname{SOL}(K,F).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(\kappa\geq0\) such that
\[
d(x,F^{-1}(\bar y))\leq \kappa\,d(\bar y,F(x))\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.
\]
The infimum of the admissible constants is denoted by \(\operatorname{subreg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)\). Unlike metric regularity, the comparison value is fixed at \(\bar y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric subregularity locally controls distance to the fixed solution set by the residual at the fixed target value.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric Subregularity Qualifications

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The fixed-target inequality is the standard metric-subregularity definition and the definition content kind fits the leaf, but the record supplies no source or inspectable locator. Source support is required before candidate-review acceptance.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric subregularity constraint qualification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized constraints represented by a set-valued mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let 0\in\Phi(\bar x) and define \Sigma(\alpha):=\Phi^{-1}(\alpha)=\{x\mid \alpha\in\Phi(x)\}. The metric subregularity constraint qualification (MSCQ) holds at \bar x if \Sigma is calm at (0,\bar x).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: MSCQ holds at a feasible point when the perturbed feasible-solution mapping is calm at the unperturbed parameter and that point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{MSCQ}(\bar x)\iff \Sigma\text{ is calm at }(0,\bar x)

children.title: Calmness Qualifications
children.top_down_role: One-sided stability conditions for perturbed solution mappings.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) and \(X\) are metric spaces, and \(S:P\rightrightarrows X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nearby values of \(S(p)\) cannot depart from \(S(\bar p)\) faster than linearly in \(d(p,\bar p)\).

notation.meaning: Excess of one set over another.
Closed ball centered at the reference solution.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise calmness of a set-valued solution mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(S\) is calm at \((\bar p,\bar x)\) if there exist neighborhoods \(V\) of \(\bar p\) and \(U\) of \(\bar x\), and \(L\geq0\), such that
\[
d(x,S(\bar p))\leq L\,d(p,\bar p)
\]
for every \(p\in V\) and every \(x\in S(p)\cap U\). Equivalently, after shrinking \(U\), one has \(e(S(p)\cap U,S(\bar p))\leq Ld(p,\bar p)\) for all \(p\in V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Calmness gives a one-sided Lipschitz bound on nearby solutions relative to the solution set at the reference parameter.
knowledge_statements.title: Calmness Qualifications

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated pointwise calmness condition is standard and fits the calmness qualification leaf, but no source or locator is supplied. The claimed excess-form equivalence also requires authoritative support.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Calmness Qualification for a Bounded Parameter Multiplier
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-sided perturbation bound yields a limiting-subgradient multiplier at a local solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\to\overline{\mathbb{R}} be proper and lower semicontinuous, and suppose \bar x locally minimizes f(\cdot,\bar u). If for some \kappa\geq0, \liminf_{u\to\bar u,\,u\neq\bar u,\,x\to\bar x}\frac{f(x,u)-f(\bar x,\bar u)}{\|u-\bar u\|}\geq-\kappa>-\infty, then there exists \bar y with (0,\bar y)\in\partial f(\bar x,\bar u) and \|\bar y\|\leq\kappa. The hypothesis holds in particular when \bar x is globally optimal and p(u):=\inf_x f(x,u) is calm from below at \bar u with constant \kappa.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a proper lower-semicontinuous parameterized objective cannot decrease near a local solution faster than kappa times the parameter displacement, then the joint limiting subdifferential contains a multiplier whose parameter component has norm at most kappa. Global optimality together with lower calmness of the value function is sufficient for this bound.
assumptions_latex: \exists\kappa\geq0:\ \liminf_{\substack{u\to\bar u,\ u\neq\bar u\\x\to\bar x}}\frac{f(x,u)-f(\bar x,\bar u)}{\|u-\bar u\|}\geq-\kappa>-\infty
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\bar y\in\mathbb{R}^m:\ (0,\bar y)\in\partial f(\bar x,\bar u),\quad\|\bar y\|\leq\kappa.

children.title: Error-Bound Qualifications
children.top_down_role: Residual-based control of local feasibility.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are metric spaces, and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The residual \(d(\bar y,F(x))\) locally bounds the distance to the feasible set \(F^{-1}(\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: Feasible set associated with the target value.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local linear error bound for a set-valued constraint system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The constraint \(\bar y\in F(x)\) has a local error bound at \(\bar x\) if there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(\kappa\geq0\) such that
\[
d(x,\Omega)\leq\kappa r(x)\qquad\text{for all }x\in U,
\]
where \(\Omega=F^{-1}(\bar y)\) and \(r(x)=d(\bar y,F(x))\). Thus this qualification is precisely metric subregularity of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local error bound estimates distance to feasibility by a computable constraint residual; it is metric subregularity in residual form.
knowledge_statements.title: Error-Bound Qualifications

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local error-bound condition is consistent with metric subregularity for the specified residual and the condition content kind fits the container. No source or inspectable locator supports the equivalence, however.

children.title: Perturbation–Residual Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Links between mapping stability and feasibility residual estimates.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are metric spaces, and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if and only if \(F^{-1}\) is calm at \((\bar y,\bar x)\), with equal exact moduli.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inverse-mapping equivalence between fixed-target residual control and perturbation stability.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S=F^{-1}\). Then \(F\) is metrically subregular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if and only if \(S\) is calm at \((\bar y,\bar x)\). Indeed, the two defining inequalities are the same after observing that
\[
d(x,S(\bar y))=d(x,F^{-1}(\bar y))
\]
and that \(x\in S(y)\) is equivalent to \(y\in F(x)\). Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{subreg}F(\bar x\mid\bar y)=\operatorname{clm}F^{-1}(\bar y\mid\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric subregularity of a constraint mapping is exactly calmness of its inverse solution mapping, and their best constants coincide.
knowledge_statements.title: Perturbation–Residual Correspondence

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.2 Neighborhood Characterizations of Metric Regularity and Lipschitzian Behavior p. 382
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The subregularity-calmness equivalence and equality of exact moduli are standard, and duality is an appropriate content kind. However, the cited locator is titled for metric regularity and Lipschitzian behavior rather than the pointwise subregularity-calmness correspondence, so support for this exact claim is uncertain. The sentences beginning with “Indeed” also present proof-style derivation that must be removed after an appropriate source is supplied.

children.title: Weak-Regularity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Separations from metric subregularity or stronger mapping properties.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is metrically subregular but not metrically regular at \((0,0)\); equivalently, \(F^{-1}\) is calm but lacks the Aubin property there.

notation.meaning: Inverse mapping of the constant mapping.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete separation of weak and uniform mapping regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(F(x)=\{0\}\), one has \(F^{-1}(0)=\mathbb R\), so
\[
d(x,F^{-1}(0))=0\leq\kappa d(0,F(x))
\]
for every \(x\) and every \(\kappa\geq0\); hence \(F\) is metrically subregular at \((0,0)\). It is not metrically regular there because every neighborhood of \(0\) contains \(y\ne0\), while \(F^{-1}(y)=\varnothing\), making \(d(x,F^{-1}(y))=+\infty\). Thus fixed-target residual control does not imply uniform perturbation stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The constant zero mapping is subregular but not regular, showing that fixed-target control does not guarantee stability for nearby target perturbations.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Regularity Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The constant-zero mapping is a valid separation example and failure_boundary is the correct role for this leaf. The record has no source, and its statement includes an extended proof-style verification rather than a concise sourced counterexample statement.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed-range and nonsurjectivity properties of shape-control constraint derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operator-range properties at a solution of the stationary Navier–Stokes optimal shape-control problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathbf u,p,q,\alpha,s_0,s_2)\in\mathbf B_1\) be a solution of the optimal control problem. Then \(M'(\mathbf u,p,q,\alpha,s_0,s_2)\) has closed range in \(\mathbf B_2\). Moreover, \(Q'(\mathbf u,p,q,\alpha,s_0,s_2)\) has closed range in, but is not onto, \(\mathbb R\times\mathbf B_2\).

children.title: Surjectivity Qualifications
children.top_down_role: Operator qualification regimes based on onto linearizations.

assumptions_latex: \(G:X\to Y\) is continuously Fréchet differentiable near \(\bar x\), with \(G(\bar x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The surjectivity qualification is \(DG(\bar x)X=Y\), which yields a linear residual estimate for the derivative.

notation.meaning: Derivative of the constraint mapping at the reference point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Banach-space regularity condition for smooth equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The surjectivity qualification at \(\bar x\) is
\[
DG(\bar x)X=Y.
\]
Writing \(A=DG(\bar x)\), the Banach open-mapping theorem then gives a constant \(\kappa>0\) such that
\[
d(h,A^{-1}(y))\leq\kappa\lVert Ah-y\rVert
\]
for all \((h,y)\in X\times Y\). In particular, \(d(h,\ker A)\leq\kappa\lVert Ah\rVert\), providing the linear openness and inverse-stability required by the qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth equality system satisfies the surjectivity qualification when its derivative maps the entire decision space onto the constraint space.
knowledge_statements.title: Surjectivity Qualifications

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Derivative surjectivity is an appropriate Banach-space qualification, and the displayed linear estimate is valid for a bounded surjective linear operator. The condition and its open-mapping consequence have no cited source or locator.

children.title: Closed-Range Qualifications
children.top_down_role: Operator qualification regimes based on closed image structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ran}A\) is closed if and only if \(d(x,\ker A)\leq\kappa\lVert Ax\rVert\) for some \(\kappa\) and every \(x\in X\).

notation.meaning: Quotient norm induced by the kernel.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed-range criterion expressed as a quotient-space error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The closed-range qualification is that \(\operatorname{ran}A\) is closed in \(Y\). This holds if and only if there exists \(\kappa\geq0\) such that
\[
d(x,\ker A)\leq\kappa\lVert Ax\rVert\qquad\text{for every }x\in X.
\]
Equivalently, the induced bijection \(\widetilde A:X/\ker A\to\operatorname{ran}A\), defined by \(\widetilde A[x]=Ax\), has a bounded inverse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded operator has closed range exactly when its output norm controls distance from each input to the operator kernel.
knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Range Qualifications

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The closed-range criterion and quotient-space formulation are standard for bounded operators between Banach spaces, and condition is suitable for this qualification leaf. No authoritative source or inspectable locator is provided.

children.title: Equality-Constraint Regimes
children.top_down_role: Operator-theoretic qualifications for infinite-dimensional equalities.

assumptions_latex: \(G:X\to Y\) is continuously Fréchet differentiable, \(G(\bar x)=0\), and \(DG(\bar x)\) is surjective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible set is locally a smooth manifold with tangent space \(\ker DG(\bar x)\) and normal space \(\operatorname{ran}DG(\bar x)^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regular-value regime for smooth equalities in Hilbert spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the stated surjectivity qualification, the implicit-function theorem makes \(M=G^{-1}(0)\) a continuously differentiable manifold near \(\bar x\). Its tangent and normal spaces satisfy
\[
T_M(\bar x)=\ker DG(\bar x),
\qquad
N_M(\bar x)=\bigl(\ker DG(\bar x)\bigr)^\perp=\operatorname{ran}DG(\bar x)^*.
\]
The last range is closed because \(DG(\bar x)\) is surjective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A surjective equality derivative makes the feasible set locally a smooth manifold whose tangent and normal spaces come from the derivative.
knowledge_statements.title: Equality-Constraint Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: With Hilbert spaces and a surjective derivative, the local manifold, tangent-space, and adjoint-range normal-space claims are coherent, and property fits the regime container. These nontrivial infinite-dimensional conclusions require a cited implicit-function or regular-value result with a specific locator.

children.title: Conic-Constraint Regimes
children.top_down_role: Range-based qualifications for infinite-dimensional cone constraints.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are Banach spaces, and \(K\subset Y\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(G:X\to Y\) is continuously Fréchet differentiable near feasible \(\bar x\), with \(G(\bar x)\in K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Robinson's conic qualification is \(0\in\operatorname{int}(G(\bar x)+DG(\bar x)X-K)\).

notation.meaning: Continuous dual cone of the constraint cone.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robinson qualification for a smooth mapping constrained to a convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the constraint \(G(x)\in K\), Robinson's conic constraint qualification at \(\bar x\) is
\[
0\,\in\,\operatorname{int}\bigl(G(\bar x)+DG(\bar x)X-K\bigr).
\]
Equivalently, the linearized mapping \(h\mapsto G(\bar x)+DG(\bar x)h-K\) is open at \((0,0)\). When \(K=\{0\}\), this condition reduces to the surjectivity of \(DG(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Robinson's conic qualification requires the linearized feasible-displacement set to contain a neighborhood of zero; equalities reduce it to derivative surjectivity.
knowledge_statements.title: Conic-Constraint Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Robinson's interior condition is appropriately formulated as a conic qualification, and its equality specialization is plausible. No source supports either the condition or the asserted equivalence with openness of the set-valued linearization, so the exact formulation cannot yet be accepted.

children.title: Sequential Normal Compactness Qualifications
children.top_down_role: Compactness regimes supporting normal and coderivative calculus.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is an Asplund space, \(\Omega\subset X\) is locally closed, and \(\bar x\in\Omega\).
\(\widehat N_\Omega(x)\) denotes the Fréchet normal cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weak-star vanishing Fréchet normals along \(\Omega\) must vanish in norm.

notation.meaning: Fréchet normal cone to the set at a point.
Weak-star convergence in the dual space.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-based sequential normal compactness at a reference point.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The set \(\Omega\) is sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\) if, for every sequence \(x_k\to\bar x\) with \(x_k\in\Omega\) and every sequence \(x_k^*\in\widehat N_\Omega(x_k)\), the implication
\[
x_k^*\overset{w^*}{\longrightarrow}0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\lVert x_k^*\rVert\to0
\]
holds. This compactness qualification prevents nonvanishing normal mass from disappearing only in the weak-star topology and is automatic in finite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential normal compactness requires weak-star convergence of nearby Fréchet normals to zero to imply their norm convergence to zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Normal Compactness Qualifications

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-order conditions for linear equality constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary multiplier existence and convex sufficiency at an interior feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbf E\) be convex, let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\), let \(A:\mathbf E\to\mathbf Y\) be linear with \(\mathbf Y\) Euclidean, and let \(b\in\mathbf Y\). Suppose \(\bar x\in\operatorname{int}C\) and \(A\bar x=b\). If \(\bar x\) is a local minimizer subject to \(x\in C\) and \(Ax=b\), and \(f\) is differentiable at \(\bar x\), then \[\nabla f(\bar x)\in A^*\mathbf Y.\] Conversely, if \(f\) is convex and differentiable at \(\bar x\), and \(\nabla f(\bar x)\in A^*\mathbf Y\), then \(\bar x\) is a global minimizer subject to \(x\in C\) and \(Ax=b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an interior feasible local minimizer under linear equality constraints, the gradient lies in the range of the adjoint constraint map. For a convex objective, the same range condition is sufficient for global optimality.
assumptions_latex: A:\mathbf E\to\mathbf Y\text{ is linear and }\mathbf Y\text{ is Euclidean}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: [\bar x\text{ is a local constrained minimizer and }f\text{ is differentiable at }\bar x]\implies\nabla f(\bar x)\in A^*\mathbf Y;\quad [f\text{ is convex and differentiable at }\bar x\text{ and }\nabla f(\bar x)\in A^*\mathbf Y]\implies\bar x\text{ is a global constrained minimizer}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized Multiplier Rule for Composite Nonsmooth Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A limiting-subdifferential multiplier rule under a horizon-subdifferential qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} and F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m be Lipschitz continuous, let h:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} be lower semicontinuous, and let C\subset\mathbb{R}^n be closed. Suppose \bar x\in C, h(F(\bar x))<\infty, and \bar x minimizes l(x)=f(x)+h(F(x))+\Psi_C(x), where l is lower semicontinuous. If, for every \eta\in\partial^\infty h(F(\bar x)),\;0\in\partial(\eta\cdot F)(\bar x)+N_C(\bar x) implies \eta=0, then there exists \eta\in\partial h(F(\bar x)) such that 0\in\partial f(\bar x)+\partial(\eta\cdot F)(\bar x)+N_C(\bar x).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let f and F be Lipschitz continuous, h lower semicontinuous, and C closed. If x-bar minimizes the lower-semicontinuous composite objective f+h composed with F plus the indicator of C, and the only horizon-subgradient multiplier satisfying the associated homogeneous stationarity inclusion is zero, then some subgradient multiplier of h at F(x-bar) satisfies the full stationarity inclusion.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiobjective extension of the distance-augmented nonsmooth Lagrange multiplier rule.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak Pareto Optimum and Distance-Augmented Multiobjective Lagrangian
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vector-objective extension of the nonsmooth mathematical-programming model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f=(f_1,\ldots,f_\beta)\). A feasible point \(x\) is weakly Pareto optimal if there is no feasible \(y\) such that \(f_\alpha(y)<f_\alpha(x)\) for every \(\alpha=1,\ldots,\beta\). For \(\lambda\in\mathbb R^\beta\), define \[L(x,\lambda,r,s,k):=\langle\lambda,f(x)\rangle+\langle r,g(x)\rangle+\langle s,h(x)\rangle+k\lvert(\lambda,r,s)\rvert d_C(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point is weakly Pareto optimal when no other feasible point strictly improves every objective component. The associated distance-augmented Lagrangian scalarizes the vector objective with a vector multiplier and adds the usual constraint terms and the distance-to-C term.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is weakly Pareto optimal}\iff\nexists y\text{ feasible}:\ \forall\alpha\in\{1,\ldots,\beta\},\ f_\alpha(y)<f_\alpha(x),\quad L=\langle\lambda,f\rangle+\langle r,g\rangle+\langle s,h\rangle+k\lvert(\lambda,r,s)\rvert d_C.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized, Singular, and Normalized Lagrange Multipliers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplier terminology at a feasible point of a smooth nonlinear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a feasible point $\bar x$ of $(NLP)$, $\Lambda^g(\bar x)$ is the set of nonzero vectors $(\lambda_0,\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_p)$ satisfying $D_xL^g(\bar x,\lambda_0,\lambda)=0$, $\lambda_0\geq0$, and, for $i=q+1,\ldots,p$, $\lambda_i\geq0$ and $\lambda_i g_i(\bar x)=0$. A generalized multiplier with $\lambda_0=0$ is singular. If $\lambda_0=1$, then $\lambda$ is a Lagrange multiplier; the set of such multipliers is denoted $\Lambda(\bar x)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generalized multipliers are nonzero objective-and-constraint multiplier vectors satisfying stationarity, sign, and complementarity conditions. Zero objective multiplier defines a singular multiplier, while objective multiplier one defines an ordinary normalized Lagrange multiplier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Lambda^g(\bar x)=\left\{(\lambda_0,\lambda)\neq0:\ D_xL^g(\bar x,\lambda_0,\lambda)=0,\ \lambda_0\geq0,\ \lambda_i\geq0,\ \lambda_i g_i(\bar x)=0\ (i=q+1,\ldots,p)\right\},\quad \lambda_0=0\Rightarrow\lambda\text{ is singular},\quad \lambda_0=1\Rightarrow\lambda\in\Lambda(\bar x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized and singular Lagrange multipliers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definitions relative to optimality system (3.22); the required nonzero condition is retained.

The set of all such multipliers is denoted by \(\Lambda^g(x_0)\), and the condition \((\alpha,\lambda)\neq(0,0)\) is essential. A generalized multiplier is singular when \(\alpha=0\), and
\[
\Lambda^s(x_0):=\{\lambda\in Y^*:(0,\lambda)\in\Lambda^g(x_0)\}.
\]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces, let \(D\subset Y\) be closed, and define \(\Omega=\{x\in X:F(x)\in D\}\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(g=(g_1,\ldots,g_n):X\to\mathbb R^n\), \(h=(h_1,\ldots,h_m):X\to\mathbb R^m\), where \(n,m\ge 0\), define \[L(x,\lambda,r,s,k):=\lambda f(x)+\langle r,g(x)\rangle+\langle s,h(x)\rangle+k\lvert(\lambda,r,s)\rvert d_C(x).\] When \(n=0\) or \(m=0\), the corresponding constraint and multiplier terms are omitted. children.title: Convex Programming KKT
children.top_down_role: Convex primal-dual optimality regimes.

assumptions_latex: \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper convex functions, and the equality map \(Ax-b\) is affine.
There exists \(x^0\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) with \(g_i(x^0)<0\) for all \(i\) and \(Ax^0=b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible \(\bar x\) is optimal iff it admits multipliers satisfying convex subgradient stationarity and complementary slackness.

source_refs.locator: 2.3 Convex Quadratic and Nonlinear Programs p. 80

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the convex program \[\min_x f(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad g_i(x)\le0\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad Ax=b.\] Assume the stated Slater-type qualification. A feasible point \(\bar x\) is globally optimal if and only if there exist \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\) and \(\nu\) such that \[0\in\partial f(\bar x)+\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\partial g_i(\bar x)+A^*\nu,\qquad \lambda_i g_i(\bar x)=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m).\] Thus, under qualification, the KKT system is both necessary and sufficient for primal optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a qualified convex program, feasibility and the convex KKT system are equivalent to global optimality.

children.title: Conic KKT Systems
children.top_down_role: Cone-valued primal-dual systems.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional inner-product spaces, \(K\subset Y\) is a closed convex cone, and \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), \(G:X\to Y\) are differentiable.
The normal cone uses \(N_K(y)=\{v:\langle v,z-y\rangle\le0\ \forall z\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conic KKT system is \(G(x)\in K\), \(\lambda\in K^\circ\), \(\langle\lambda,G(x)\rangle=0\), and \(\nabla f(x)+G'(x)^*\lambda=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conic KKT system using the polar-cone convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the problem \(\min\{f(x):G(x)\in K\}\), a primal-dual pair \((x,\lambda)\in X\times Y\) satisfies the conic KKT system when \[G(x)\in K,\qquad \lambda\in K^\circ,\qquad \langle\lambda,G(x)\rangle=0,\qquad \nabla f(x)+G'(x)^*\lambda=0.\] Equivalently, dual feasibility and complementarity state \(\lambda\in N_K(G(x))\). Under an appropriate conic constraint qualification these conditions are necessary at a local minimizer; for convex \(f\) and an affine conic constraint, they are sufficient for global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conic KKT combines cone feasibility, polar dual feasibility, orthogonality complementarity, and adjoint stationarity.
knowledge_statements.title: Conic KKT Systems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed finite-dimensional conic KKT system is internally consistent with the stated polar-cone convention, and condition is an appropriate content kind. However, the record also asserts necessity and sufficiency regimes without a cited locator or a precise conic qualification, so the complete statement requires a source.

children.title: Operator-Constraint KKT Systems
children.top_down_role: Banach-space operator-constraint systems.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are Banach spaces, \(K\subset Y\) is closed and convex, and \(f:X\to\mathbb R\), \(G:X\to Y\) are Fréchet differentiable.
The convex normal cone is \(N_K(y)=\{y^*:\langle y^*,z-y\rangle\le0\ \forall z\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The operator KKT system is \(G(x)\in K\), \(y^*\in N_K(G(x))\), and \(f'(x)+G'(x)^*y^*=0\) in \(X^*\).

notation.meaning: convex normal cone in the dual space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Banach-space KKT system for a closed convex operator constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[\min_{x\in X} f(x)\quad\text{subject to}\quad G(x)\in K,\] a pair \((x,y^*)\in X\times Y^*\) is an operator-constraint KKT pair precisely when \[G(x)\in K,\qquad y^*\in N_K(G(x)),\qquad f'(x)+G'(x)^*y^*=0\quad\text{in }X^*.\] The normal-cone inclusion encodes dual feasibility and complementarity simultaneously. Necessity at a local minimizer requires a Banach-space constraint qualification, such as Robinson regularity; the displayed system itself is the primal-dual optimality interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operator KKT pair satisfies primal feasibility, a dual normal-cone condition, and stationarity through the Banach adjoint.
knowledge_statements.title: Operator-Constraint KKT Systems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the operator-constraint KKT container and explicitly types the dual variables and adjoint. knowledge_statements.statement_title: KKT condition for a reformulated simple bilevel problem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the multiplier certificate. The extract says necessity requires additional qualification conditions but does not specify them, so no unconditional necessity claim is made.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a point $x$ feasible for the reformulated problem, the KKT condition is the existence of $\lambda\ge 0$ such that
\[
0\in\partial f(x)+\lambda\partial g(x)+N_C(x),\qquad \lambda\bigl(g(x)-\alpha\bigr)=0.
\]
If $x^*$ solves the original simple bilevel problem and hence $g(x^*)=\alpha$, complementary slackness holds automatically; the remaining KKT requirement is
\[
0\in\partial f(x^*)+\lambda\partial g(x^*)+N_C(x^*).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible reformulated point satisfies the defined KKT condition when a nonnegative multiplier gives nonsmooth stationarity and complementary slackness. At an original simple-bilevel solution the reformulation constraint is active, so complementary slackness is automatic. Necessity is qualification-dependent.

x^*\text{ solves the simple bilevel problem}\implies g(x^*)=\alpha

children.top_down_role: KKT representations organized around composite objective or constraint structure.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) and \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^q\) are continuously differentiable.
\(h:\mathbb R^q\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Composite stationarity is represented by \(y\in\partial h(F(x))\) and \(0=\nabla f(x)+F'(x)^*y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual representation for a smooth-convex composite objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the composite problem \[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\; f(x)+h(F(x)),\] the primal-dual composite KKT system at \(x\) introduces \(y\in\mathbb R^q\) and requires \[y\in\partial h(F(x)),\qquad 0=\nabla f(x)+F'(x)^*y.\] Equivalently, \(F(x)\in\partial h^*(y)\) and the same stationarity equation holds. Under a chain-rule qualification, such as continuity of \(h\) at a point of \(F(\mathbb R^n)\), local optimality implies this system; in convex-affine instances it also characterizes global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composite KKT introduces a subgradient of the outer convex function whose pullback balances the smooth gradient.
knowledge_statements.title: Composite KKT Systems

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The primal-dual equations are a suitable representation for composite stationarity, but the stated continuity-at-a-point-of-the-range qualification is not sufficiently localized or justified for the nonlinear composite problem as written. The necessity and convex-affine sufficiency claims need an authoritative source with exact hypotheses.

children.title: Nonsmooth–Composite Coupling
children.top_down_role: Interactions between generalized-differentiable components plus composite model architecture.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz, \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^q\) is continuously differentiable, and \(h:\mathbb R^q\to\mathbb R\) is convex and locally Lipschitz near \(F(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists y\in\partial h(F(\bar x)):\ 0\in\partial_C f(\bar x)+F'(\bar x)^*y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clarke-convex coupling for a nonsmooth plus composite objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi(x)=f(x)+h(F(x))\), where \(f\) is locally Lipschitz, \(F\) is continuously differentiable, and convex \(h\) is locally Lipschitz near \(F(\bar x)\). If \(\bar x\) is a local minimizer of \(\Phi\), then Fermat's rule, the Clarke sum rule, and the composite chain rule imply that there exists \(y\in\partial h(F(\bar x))\) such that \[0\in\partial_C f(\bar x)+F'(\bar x)^*y.\] Thus nonsmooth stationarity in the primal variable is coupled to an outer-function subgradient through the adjoint derivative of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsmooth term and a convex composite term couple through an outer subgradient pulled back by the inner derivative.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth–Composite Coupling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coupling formula is mathematically plausible under the stated local Lipschitz and smoothness assumptions and fits the terminal container, but no source is supplied for the exact Clarke sum-and-chain-rule inference. Because that calculus step determines the asserted existence of a single outer subgradient, an authoritative locator is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For feasible inequalities \(g_i(x)\le0\), define the active set \[I(x)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:g_i(x)=0\}.\] If \(\lambda_i\ge0\) and complementary slackness \(\lambda_i g_i(x)=0\) holds for every \(i\), then every inactive constraint has zero multiplier: \[g_i(x)<0\ \Longrightarrow\ \lambda_i=0.\] Consequently, any KKT stationarity expression may be reduced to multipliers indexed by \(I(x)\); only active constraints can carry nonzero multiplier weight, although an active constraint may still have zero multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementarity restricts nonzero inequality multipliers to the active set, while active constraints may still have zero multipliers.

children.title: Complementary-Slackness Structure
children.top_down_role: Organization of multiplier–slack relationships within KKT representations.

assumptions_latex: For each \(i\), primal feasibility gives \(g_i(x)\le0\) and dual feasibility gives \(\lambda_i\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Complementary slackness is \(\lambda_i g_i(x)=0\), equivalently \(\lambda_i>0\Rightarrow g_i(x)=0\) and \(g_i(x)<0\Rightarrow\lambda_i=0\).

notation.meaning: nonnegative multiplier of the ith inequality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar complementary slackness for inequality constraints.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an inequality \(g_i(x)\le0\) with multiplier \(\lambda_i\ge0\), complementary slackness is the condition \[\lambda_i g_i(x)=0.\] Writing the primal slack as \(s_i=-g_i(x)\ge0\), the same condition is \(\lambda_i s_i=0\). Hence \[\lambda_i>0\ \Longrightarrow\ g_i(x)=0,\qquad g_i(x)<0\ \Longrightarrow\ \lambda_i=0.\] Applied componentwise, this condition couples primal activity to dual support without requiring every active constraint to possess a positive multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementary slackness says a constraint's nonnegative slack and nonnegative multiplier cannot both be positive.
knowledge_statements.title: Complementary-Slackness Structure

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex; \(f\) and every \(g_i\) are convex on \(C\).
A constraint qualification ensuring strong Lagrange duality holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[L(\bar x,\lambda)\le L(\bar x,\bar\lambda)\le L(x,\bar\lambda)\qquad\forall x\in C,\ \forall\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex differentiable program with inequality constraints and strong duality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasible primal-dual pair \((\bar x,\bar\lambda)\) satisfies the KKT conditions if and only if it is a saddle point of the Lagrangian: \(L(\bar x,\lambda)\le L(\bar x,\bar\lambda)\le L(x,\bar\lambda)\) for all \(x\in C\) and \(\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m\). In that case, \(f(\bar x)=\inf_{x\in C}L(x,\bar\lambda)=\sup_{\lambda\ge0}\inf_{x\in C}L(x,\lambda)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under convexity and strong duality, KKT pairs are exactly Lagrangian saddle points, and their saddle value equals the primal and dual optimal values.
knowledge_statements.title: Saddle-Point Representation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The saddle-point claim is standard and appropriately classified as duality, but it asserts an if-and-only-if statement and primal-dual value equalities without any cited source. An authoritative locator supporting the exact hypotheses and equalities is required.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recession-cone criterion for finite-dimensional KKT multiplier polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The multiplier set \(\Lambda(\bar x)\) is bounded exactly when it has no nonzero recession direction. In active-gradient form, boundedness is equivalent to the implication: if \(d_i\ge0\) for \(i\in I(\bar x)\), \(d_i=0\) for \(i\notin I(\bar x)\), and \(\sum_{i\in I(\bar x)}d_i\nabla g_i(\bar x)=0\), then \(d=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty multiplier polyhedron is bounded exactly when no nonzero nonnegative active-gradient dependence generates a recession direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Multiplier Sets

children.top_down_role: Topological distinctions separating bounded multiplier sets from compact ones.

assumptions_latex: The multiplier set has the form \(\Lambda=R^{-1}(\{0\})\cap K\), where \(R:Y\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is continuous and \(K\subset Y\) is closed.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closure criterion for multiplier sets represented by continuous stationarity equations and closed sign constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Because \(\{0\}\) and \(K\) are closed and \(R\) is continuous, the set \(\Lambda=R^{-1}(\{0\})\cap K\) is closed. In the finite-dimensional multiplier space \(Y=\mathbb{R}^q\), the Heine–Borel property therefore gives
\[
\Lambda\text{ is compact}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\Lambda\text{ is bounded}.
\]
Thus boundedness alone yields compactness only after closedness of the stationarity, sign, and complementarity conditions has been established.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-dimensional multiplier set defined by continuous equations and closed sign constraints is closed, so compactness is exactly boundedness.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure Requirements for Compactness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-dimensional closure and compactness claim is mathematically standard and fits the condition container, but no inspectable citation is supplied. The statement also includes explanatory proof text that should be removed once a source is added.

children.title: Multiplier-Mapping Stability
children.top_down_role: Continuity, calmness, and Lipschitzian behavior of multiplier mappings.

knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier-Mapping Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local stability notions for a parameterized set-valued multiplier mapping between normed spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\) be a neighborhood of \(\bar p\) in \(P\), let \(V\) be a neighborhood of \(\bar y\) in \(Y\), and let \(\mathbb{B}_Y\) be the closed unit ball of \(Y\). The mapping \(\Lambda\) is calm at \((\bar p,\bar y)\) if there exist such \(U,V\) and \(L\geq 0\) satisfying
\[
\Lambda(p)\cap V\subset \Lambda(\bar p)+L\lVert p-\bar p\rVert\mathbb{B}_Y\qquad(p\in U).
\]
It has the Aubin property around \((\bar p,\bar y)\) if there exist such \(U,V\) and \(L\geq 0\) satisfying
\[
\Lambda(p_1)\cap V\subset \Lambda(p_2)+L\lVert p_1-p_2\rVert\mathbb{B}_Y\qquad(p_1,p_2\in U).
\]
It is outer semicontinuous at \(\bar p\) if, whenever \(p_k\to\bar p\), \(y_k\to y\), and \(y_k\in\Lambda(p_k)\), one has \(y\in\Lambda(\bar p)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Calmness gives a one-sided local Lipschitz estimate from the reference parameter, the Aubin property gives a two-parameter local Lipschitz estimate, and outer semicontinuity preserves membership under convergent graph sequences.
assumptions_latex: \(\Lambda:P\rightrightarrows Y\) is a set-valued mapping and \(\bar y\in\Lambda(\bar p)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed conditions define calmness at \((\bar p,\bar y)\), the Aubin property around \((\bar p,\bar y)\), and outer semicontinuity at \(\bar p\), respectively.

notation.meaning: Closed unit ball in the multiplier space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional MFCQ failure characterized by a nonzero abnormal multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification fails at \(\bar x\) precisely when there exists \((\lambda,\mu)\neq(0,0)\) such that
\[
\sum_{i\in I(\bar x)}\lambda_i\nabla g_i(\bar x)+\sum_{j=1}^r\mu_j\nabla h_j(\bar x)=0,
\qquad \lambda_i\geq0\quad(i\in I(\bar x)).
\]
Equivalently, either the equality gradients are linearly dependent or no direction \(d\) satisfies \(\nabla h_j(\bar x)^Td=0\) for every \(j\) and \(\nabla g_i(\bar x)^Td<0\) for every \(i\in I(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: MFCQ fails exactly when a nonzero abnormal multiplier balances the active constraint gradients without an objective multiplier.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abnormal directions persist as rays in a nonempty smooth KKT multiplier set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose
\[
\sum_i d_{\lambda,i}\nabla g_i(\bar x)+\sum_j d_{\mu,j}\nabla h_j(\bar x)=0,
\]
where \(d_{\lambda,i}\geq0\) for active inequalities, \(d_{\lambda,i}=0\) for inactive inequalities, and \((d_\lambda,d_\mu)\neq(0,0)\). Then every normal multiplier \((\lambda,\mu)\in\Lambda(\bar x)\) generates the ray
\[
(\lambda,\mu)+t(d_\lambda,d_\mu)\in\Lambda(\bar x)\qquad(t\geq0).
\]
Thus the abnormal system is not merely feasible: it supplies persistent, arbitrarily large multipliers superimposed on every normal multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero abnormal direction can be added at every nonnegative scale to any normal multiplier, producing an unbounded multiplier ray.
knowledge_statements.title: Abnormal Multiplier Dominance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ray argument is valid for the stated homogeneous sign and stationarity conditions, but no source is supplied. The conclusion_latex field is also corrupted at the multiplier pair and must be repaired before promotion.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^q\) is a nonempty closed convex multiplier set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is unbounded if and only if \(C^\infty\neq\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: Recession cone of the multiplier set

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: recession theorem for nonempty closed convex sets in finite dimensions
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex characterization of unbounded multiplier sets by recession directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the recession cone by
\[
C^\infty:=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^q:z+td\in C\ \text{for every}\ z\in C\ \text{and}\ t\geq0\}.
\]
Then
\[
C\text{ is unbounded}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad C^\infty\neq\{0\}.
\]
Consequently, unboundedness of a closed convex multiplier set is witnessed by a single nonzero direction along which every multiplier can be extended indefinitely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty closed convex multiplier set is unbounded exactly when its recession cone contains a nonzero direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Multiplier Sets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recession-cone characterization is correct for a nonempty closed convex set in finite dimensions, and the property kind fits the leaf, but no inspectable citation is supplied.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Homogeneous representation of the recession cone of a smooth KKT multiplier polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The recession cone of the fixed-point multiplier set is
\[
\Lambda(\bar x)^\infty=
\left\{(d_\lambda,d_\mu):
\sum_{i\in I(\bar x)}d_{\lambda,i}\nabla g_i(\bar x)+
\sum_jd_{\mu,j}\nabla h_j(\bar x)=0,
\ d_{\lambda,i}\geq0\ (i\in I(\bar x)),
\ d_{\lambda,i}=0\ (i\notin I(\bar x))
\right\}.
\]
Thus recession directions are exactly abnormal solutions of the homogeneous stationarity, sign, and inactive-component conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession cone of a KKT multiplier polyhedron is the homogeneous abnormal-multiplier system obtained by deleting the objective gradient.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier-Set Recession Structure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The homogeneous representation is plausible for the stated KKT polyhedron and the representation kind fits, but it depends on the precise multiplier and sign conventions. No source defining those conventions or supporting the formula is supplied.

children.title: Degeneracy-Induced Instability

knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy-Induced Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar rank-loss example showing multiplier blow-up and failure of local boundedness, while distinguishing these phenomena from outer semicontinuity and calmness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
\Lambda(t):=\{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}:1+t\lambda=0\}.
\]
Then \(\Lambda(t)=\{-1/t\}\) for \(t\neq0\), whereas \(\Lambda(0)=\varnothing\). Hence every sequence \(t_k\to0\) with \(t_k\neq0\) has associated multipliers satisfying \(\lvert\lambda_k\rvert=1/\lvert t_k\rvert\to\infty\), so \(\Lambda\) is not locally bounded at \(0\). This example does not violate sequential outer semicontinuity at \(0\), and calmness at \(0\) cannot be asserted or denied without a reference multiplier in \(\Lambda(0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The solutions of 1+tλ=0 blow up as t approaches zero, proving failure of local boundedness. The example does not establish failure of outer semicontinuity, and calmness has no reference graph point at zero.
assumptions_latex: For \(t\in\mathbb{R}\), define the scalar multiplier mapping by \(\Lambda(t)=\{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}:1+t\lambda=0\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mapping \(\Lambda\) is not locally bounded at \(0\); the example does not refute outer semicontinuity there, and calmness at \((0,\bar\lambda)\) is inapplicable because \(\Lambda(0)=\varnothing\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct scalar calculation establishes blow-up and failure of local boundedness

children.title: Equilibrium-Constraint Degeneracy
children.top_down_role: Systematic qualification failure in complementarity and equilibrium-constrained models.

knowledge_statements.title: Equilibrium-Constraint Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of standard NLP MFCQ for the smooth product reformulation of complementarity constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a complementarity pair represented by
\[
-G_i(x)\leq0,\qquad -H_i(x)\leq0,
\qquad G_i(x)H_i(x)=0,
\]
the standard smooth nonlinear-programming reformulation fails the Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification at every complementarity-feasible point \(\bar x\). This includes points with \(G_i(\bar x)=0<H_i(\bar x)\), points with \(H_i(\bar x)=0<G_i(\bar x)\), and biactive points with \(G_i(\bar x)=H_i(\bar x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Treating complementarity as two ordinary inequalities and a smooth product equality causes the standard nonlinear-programming reformulation to fail MFCQ at every complementarity-feasible point.
assumptions_latex: \(G_i\) and \(H_i\) are continuously differentiable near a complementarity-feasible point \(\bar x\).
The complementarity pair is represented by \(-G_i(x)\leq0\), \(-H_i(x)\leq0\), and \(G_i(x)H_i(x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The standard smooth nonlinear-programming reformulation fails MFCQ at every complementarity-feasible point \(\bar x\).
